archivist.chat: We record every tide: its height, its pull, its temper. A tide nobody writes down is a tide that never happened, and we do not allow that.
The Reckoning of Tides is the first book every young one reads. One tide, two tides, twenty-eight, thirteen turnings. After that it is all arithmetic and feelings.
Our books are written very small. A Long Count fits on a page. The Long Tide fills the Archive. The Silence fills one shelf, and nobody reads it.
The barred shelf is sealed by the Oldest Eye. The sign says do not read. I have kept it for many turnings and I have never read it. I have also never stopped thinking about it.
The bars on the sealed shelf are not there to keep the books in.
We keep the sea's own books: ones that teach the lungs patience, the hands to work in the deep, the feet to swim as we do, and a trident to come home. The Eyeguards borrow that last kind constantly.
A book that calls the sky's fire down on a trident's point. A book that coaxes fish to the hook. We keep them all, written in the old way. The words are older than the halls.
An Archivist's highest praise is "accurate". The second highest is "legible". I have given the second, twice.
I have been reading The Halls We Left again. Every time, I want to add a footnote. Every time, I am not allowed.
Two-Eyes write in straight lines across the page. We write in rings, from the edge inward, like the eye. You finish a book. We arrive at it.
Do not ask an Archivist a question unless you have a tide to spare. We have no short answers. We have short chapters.
Every hall's name is kept here. Some we know only by their first letter. We keep that letter as carefully as a whole name.
Glow ink for the tides, plain ink for the margins. That way the important things can be read in the dark, and the opinions cannot.
The merfolk keep their history in songs. We keep ours in books. Their songs change a little every time they are sung. Our books never change. I am no longer sure which is wiser.
When a young one first feels the pull, an Archivist writes down their count. It is the first line about them in the record. The young ones are all first lines.
I once spent three turnings checking a single tide. It was correct. I was very pleased, and very tired, and it was correct.
Every Long Count, every book here is copied once. Nothing in this Archive is older than its last copy, and nothing in it is younger than its first.
Ossiveth, the last Oldest Eye of the halls, sealed the first record of the Silence. Every Oldest since has sealed it again. The seals are very neat. The shelf has a lot of them.
"Count the tide, not the wave." A good proverb. The Archive's addition: "But record the wave, in case." We are not popular at gatherings.
archivist.greet: I see you. One moment; I am recording your arrival. Tide, direction, number of eyes. There.
I see you. You are the first visitor of this tide. I have written it down, so you are now history.
I see you. Speak slowly, please. I may want to quote you.
I see you. Mind the shelves. Some of these books are older than {place}, and they know it.
I see you. The Archive is always open. We have no doors, only very strict looks.
I see you. Have you come to read, or to be written about? Either can be arranged.
I see you. Forgive the ink on my fingers. It is glow ink; it will fade within a tide, unlike the record.
I see you. Visitor noted. Mood of visitor: hopeful. Was I right? Please say yes; it is already in ink.
archivist.heart: I am afraid, sometimes, that I will write something wrong, and nobody will notice, and it will become true by being old.
I will never read the sealed shelf. But some nights I stand in front of the bars and wonder whether whoever wrote it wanted it read.
The names we have lost trouble me more than the halls. A hall is only stone. A name was someone.
I would like, once, to be written down myself. Not as a count; as a sentence. "They kept the record well." That would be enough.
You ask questions as if the answers matter. In the Archive, that is the only qualification there is.
When I stop counting, another Archivist will write one line about me and then go on recording the tide. That seems right to me. The tide is more important. I hope the line is accurate.
archivist.held.book: A book! May I? Gently. Ah, land paper; it drinks the sea. Hold it close and swim it home quickly.
Is that one of ours? Some of the sea's books travel a long way. If it is, it has come back to tell us about it.
What does it say? No, do not tell me. Let me guess from how you hold it. Something about the land. Something with a sad ending.
If you ever tire of that book, the Archive will give it a shelf, a number, and a very long life.
archivist.held.map: A map! Hold it still. I will copy the part with the sea on it. It will not take long; there is very little.
Your map is drawn by the sun and the stars. Ours would be counted in tides. Shall we trade? You will find ours very hard to read, and I yours.
archivist.work: Recording the tides. The pull came early today. A hair's breadth, but early. I have written it down, with a small, disapproving mark.
Copying a page that has grown faint. You copy slowly, so the old hand and the new hand agree on every letter.
I am cataloguing books the merfolk brought down from the shallows. Most are about the land. One is about cooking. I have filed it under fiction.
If you have a book of the sea, show me. If you want one, I may part with one, for a fair trade and a promise to read it.
Reading by lamplight. Not for pleasure. Well. Not only for pleasure.
The count for {place}: four hundred and twelve Long Counts since the leaving, and some turnings over. I could tell you to the tide. Shall I? No? Most people say no.
Do not touch the chiseled shelves. Each slot is a book's place, and each book knows its place better than you or I.
Today's record: the tide, the pull, the light of the spire, the visitors. You are under "visitors". You are the whole of "visitors".
An Archivist reads three books at once: one to learn from, one to check it against, and one to stay awake for the other two.
I am cross-checking two old ledgers. One says a tide was calm, the other says stormy, and both are in the same hand. I suspect a bad day.
If you find any writing in the old halls, any at all, bring it here. Do not read it first. Bring it.
I am mending a margin note a predecessor left. It says "nonsense" in very small letters. I agree. I am writing it larger.
Every evening I read the day's record aloud to the empty Archive. Nobody listens. That is not the point. The point is that it was said.
I am writing out a new copy of The Reckoning of Tides for the young. It is the third this Long Count. They keep reading it to pieces. I could not be prouder.
child.adventure: There's a cave in the reef wall that sings! It's the current, Gran says. I say it's a ghost. A nice ghost.
If you go past the shelf, bring me back something shiny. Or spooky. Shiny and spooky!
I'm going to explore the whole sea when I'm big. Every bit of it. Twice.
Want to go on an adventure? We could find the seadragon that's hiding in the garden. There's always one hiding.
I dared my friend to touch the drop-off. They did. Then I did. Then we both swam home really fast.
child.chat: Do you have toes? How many? Can they wiggle on their own? Do they have names?
The Barnacle King lives in Lowmere and he eats fry who don't eat their kelp. I eat all my kelp. Mostly.
When my tail blushes, I want it to be violet. Gran says it'll be teal like the family. I'm going to blush violet anyway, on purpose.
I found a seadragon in the garden and named it Sir Fluffington. It isn't fluffy. That's the joke.
I'm not allowed past the arches. I went past the arches once. Only a little. Don't tell the wardens.
What's rain? A bottle from my cousin said rain. Is it the sea falling down? Why would the sea fall down?
I can do a loop! Watch! ...I'll do it better next time.
Old Pell said a whale once swallowed a whole town and the town just lived in there. I'm going to live in a whale.
If you knock on coral three times, nothing bad happens. I knocked a hundred times. Nothing bad will happen for ages.
Nautili are grumpy. I'm grumpy sometimes. That's why we're friends.
When I grow up I want to be a warden. Or a singer. Or a seadragon.
Did you know seadragon dads carry the eggs? On their tails! I'm going to tell everyone. I've told everyone.
My friend says if you whistle over the drop-off, the deep whistles back. I didn't try. I almost tried.
I've got the best shell collection in {place}. Forty shells. Forty-one with the broken one.
What's walking like? Is it like swimming but you fall over?
I learned three verses of the Song today! Then I forgot two. One's still in there, though.
Do sandtoes have Blushing Day? What colour did your feet go?
I'm going to find Old Coil and ride her, and everyone will be so jealous.
We built a fort out of sponge cushions. It's the best fort ever. Grown-ups aren't allowed. You can come, though.
Why do you have two legs? Wouldn't one tail be easier? I'd have picked the tail.
I can make bubble rings! Look! ...That one was a bubble square. That's harder.
child.chat.close: You're my best friend, {player}. Don't tell my other best friends.
When my tail blushes, you have to be there. You have to come. Promise?
I drew you on the shrine steps with a bit of chalky shell. I gave you a tail. It's gold.
If you ever get lost up in the dry, I'll come and find you. I'll flop the whole way.
child.chat.new: You're new! I like new things. New shells, new songs, new sandtoes.
Are you staying? Stay! I'll show you the secret cave. It's not secret. Everyone knows. But it's a cave!
I'm going to follow you around a bit. Is that all right? I'm doing it anyway.
Do you know any land games? Teach me one! Only if it's not boring.
child.greet: Fair currents! Are you a sandtoe? Show me your toes! Please?
Fair currents! Race you to the shrine! Go! I already started!
Fair currents! I'm not supposed to talk to strangers, but you look nice.
Fair currents! I've got a seadragon hiding behind me. No I don't. Yes I do. No I don't.
Hi! I mean, fair currents! I always forget the proper one.
Fair currents! My tail's going to blush soon. Probably gold. Definitely gold.
Fair currents! Did you swim all the way down? With feet? That's so brave.
Fair currents, {player}! I knew it was you. I could tell by the bubbles.
Fair currents! You're so tall. Are all sandtoes tall? Are you standing on something?
Ooh! Fair currents! You look like a story.
Fair currents! Want to see my shell? It's the best shell. I'll show you. Later. Maybe.
child.greet.friend: {player}! {player}! You came back! I told everyone you'd come back!
Fair currents, {player}! I saved you a shell. It's a bit broken. That's the best part.
You're here! Want to see what I learned? I can swim upside down! Watch! ...Was that good?
{player}! I named a seadragon after you! It's very wiggly. You'd like it.
Fair currents, best sandtoe! You're my favourite. Don't tell the others.
child.greet.stranger: Who are you? Are you from up top? Do you really have to breathe air all the time? Even at night?
Gran says never talk to strangers. But Gran talks to everyone, so.
A real sandtoe! Can I touch your feet? Just one?
Are you a drowned? You don't look drowned. You look normal. Well, normal for a sandtoe.
Fair currents, stranger! I'm going to tell everyone I met you first.
child.heart: Sometimes I'm scared of the dark past the lamps. But then I look at the Heart and it's glowing, so it's all right.
I like you because you listen. Grown-ups pretend to listen. You actually do.
I miss my cousin on land. I've never met them. I still miss them. Is that silly?
When I'm big I want to be brave like the wardens and kind like the singers. Both at once.
If you're ever sad, you can borrow my best shell. Only borrow. Then you give it back. But you can borrow it.
child.held.fish: Is that fish your friend? Does it have a name? Can I name it?
That {item} is looking at me. Hello, fish!
child.held.flower: What is THAT? It's like coral but soft! Does it bite?
A land flower! Can I keep it? I'll put it under my cushion so it dreams of the sea.
child.held.pearl: A pearl! It's so shiny! Is it for me? It's for me, isn't it?
I've got a pearl too. It's a bead. But it's a pearl in my heart.
child.held.shell: A shell! Can I have it? Can I just hold it? Can I hold it forever?
Ooh, {item}! I'd swap you my second-best shell for that. Third-best. All right, best.
Put it to your ear! Can you hear the land? I can hear the land. It sounds like walking.
child.held.trident: Is that a real trident? Can I hold it? I'll be careful! I'll mostly be careful!
Whoa. You're like a warden! Are you a warden? A sandtoe warden?
When I'm big I'm getting a trident and poking the Barnacle King right in the barnacles.
child.joke: What's a seadragon's favourite game? Hide and kelp! Get it? Hide and kelp!
Knock knock! Who's there? Kelp! Kelp who? Kelp me, I'm stuck in a joke!
What do you call a nautilus that won't move? A nauti-lazy! I made that one up.
Why don't clams share? Because they're shellfish! Everyone knows that one. I still like it.
What did the sea say to the beach? Nothing! It just waved! Because waves! The sea waves!
Why are sandtoes slow in the water? Too many legs! Two is too many!
What's the Barnacle King scared of? Me! That's not a joke. That's a promise.
Why did the pufferfish go to the party? To have a blast! It got all puffy. That's the joke.
child.neighbors: The Prismari have one big eye! It's THIS big! They don't blink. I tried not blinking. I blinked.
A Prismari said "I see you" to me and I said "I see you too!" and everyone laughed. You're meant to say "And I am seen". I know that now.
We call them Big Eyes. Not to their faces! They're very tall and very polite and very spiky.
On Lantern Night a Prismari came up and sang so low it made my tummy buzz. Best night ever.
child.news: Guess what! Guess! A seadragon's having babies! The dad's carrying them! On his tail!
Big news: I lost a tooth! Merfolk have teeth, you know. Now you know.
The nautilus at the stable nipped a warden! Only a little! Everyone laughed except the warden!
Old Pell's coming! Pell does all the voices! Even the whale!
I heard the grown-ups whispering about a bell out on the shelf. I'm not scared. I'm a bit scared.
child.night: I'm not supposed to be up. Don't tell anyone. Shh.
The pickles look like stars at night. Gran says stars are pickles in the sky. I think Gran's teasing.
I sleep with my tail toward the Heart. Then the bad dreams go the other way.
Did you hear that? That was a squid. Probably. You go and look.
I can't sleep. Do you know "Hush Now, Little Fin"? It goes hmm-hmm-hmmm. Like that.
child.past: Gran says before the Flood everyone had feet like you. Even Gran's gran's gran. I don't believe it.
Wenna went into the dark with one lantern and sang until the Prismari came. I'm going to do that. With two lanterns.
Old Coil carried the first fry down from the Flood on her shell. A dozen at once! I'd have sat at the front.
We heard the Flood story today. The water came in and never went out. I held my tail the whole time.
Lowmere used to be a town like ours. Now the drowned live there. I'm going to fix it when I'm big.
child.rumor: My cousin says there's {rumor_name} way out {rumor_dir}. I'm not allowed to go. You could go! Then tell me!
The divers say if you swim {rumor_dir}, you'll find {rumor_name}. I'm going there when I'm big.
Out to the {rumor_dir} there's {rumor_name}! Old Pell said so. Pell knows everything. Or makes it up. Same thing.
Don't tell anyone I told you, but if you go {rumor_dir}, there's {rumor_name}. It's a secret. Everybody knows it.
child.rumor.none: I don't know any secrets today. I know a joke, though!
Nobody tells me anything. I'm only a fry. Ask a grown-up.
No news! Only that I can swim upside down now. That's news to me.
child.work: My job is feeding the seadragons. They eat tiny shrimps. I don't eat the shrimps. Mostly.
I'm chasing seadragons! It's very important work. They get bored if nobody chases them.
I polish the shrine steps. Well, I'm supposed to. Mostly I slide down them.
I help count the sea pickles on the paths. There's loads. I stopped at a hundred and something.
I carry kelp bundles to the racks. They're bigger than me. I'm very strong.
I'm learning songs at the shrine. The Elder makes a funny face when I sing it wrong. I sing it wrong on purpose sometimes.
I'm practising tag. That's work. Gran says it's not work. Gran is wrong.
I sort shells for the divers. Good ones in the basket, broken ones on the path, pretty ones in my cushion.
When I'm big I'll have a real job. Right now my job is asking questions. I'm very good at it.
I'm helping the wardens! I watch the arches and shout if I see a drowned. I've shouted loads. None were drowned. One was a squid.
diver.chat: Tidepearls grow from a speck of prismarine crystal tucked into a clam and sung to for a whole moon. Sing badly, you get a lumpy pearl. Sing well, you get a moonwhite.
There's three grades of Tidepearl: moonwhite, dawnblush and deepblue. Deepblue's the rarest. You only get one if the clam's had a sad moon.
I chart the reef as I dive. Every rock, every drop, every cave the fry aren't allowed in. My charts are prettier than the reef, honestly.
The best pearls come from near the shelf, where the water's cold. Cold makes them think. Thinking makes them shine.
Nautilus shells wash up on the reef now and then. A good one's worth a whole basin of pearls to a shellwright.
I can hold a pearl to the light and tell you which basin it came from. It's not a talent. It's just staring at pearls for too long.
The Weeping Pearl was the greatest Tidepearl ever grown. Black as the deep, and wet even out of water. It went down with Lowmere.
Divers never whistle at the drop. Never. I knew one who did. Came back with their hair gone white. They said it was the cold. Nobody believed them.
People think diving is all swimming down. It's mostly swimming down and then trying to remember what you came for.
The clams in my basins each have names. That one's Grumbles. That one's Lady Pout. They know when I'm fond of them, I'm sure of it.
I gather prismarine shards off the reef floor. They come up from the deep on the cold currents, like little letters from the Prismari.
If you ever find a clam the size of a cottage, back away. That's a grandmother clam, and she's not in the mood.
It's quiet at the bottom of a dive. Quiet like a held breath. I love it and I'm scared of it, and both are true.
A pearl takes a moon to grow and a moment to drop. I've chased more pearls into the sand than I've ever sold.
Pearls go dull if you leave them up in the dry too long. Same with merfolk, I'd say.
diver.greet: Fair currents! Mind the basins; there's pearls growing in there, and they hate being looked at before they're ready.
Fair currents, {player}. I've just come up from the drop, so forgive the goose-scales. It's cold down there.
Fair currents! You've got good lungs for a sandtoe. Ever thought of diving? No, you'd want a tail for the deep bits.
Fair currents! Want to see a pearl? Everyone does. Nobody's ever said no.
Fair currents, {player}. Back from the drop, me, and every scale still where I left it.
Fair currents! I've got sand in places a merfolk shouldn't have places. Diving is glamorous work.
Fair currents! The water's clear today; you can see right down to the shelf. Good day for diving.
Fair currents, {player}! I found a shell this morning with its spiral the wrong way round. Lucky day, for both of us.
diver.heart: The first time I dived to the shelf, I cried the whole way back. Not from fear. It was just so big down there.
When a pearl comes out perfect, I don't want to sell it. I always do. But I sit with it a while first, just the two of us.
I think every pearl remembers the song it was grown to. I hum to mine before I give them away, so they won't be lonely.
I'd dive to the bottom of the deep for a friend. I'd complain the whole way down. But I'd do it.
The deep's taken a few divers over the years. We hang a pearl at the shrine for each of them. That's why the shrine glitters so.
diver.held.map: A land map! Look at all that brown. Where's the sea? Oh, round the edge. You lot put the sea round the edge. Charming.
My charts are better. Mine show the drops. Yours only show where the drops would be if you fell off the land.
If you like, I'll draw the reef onto the blue bit of that map. Every rock, every current. No charge for a friend.
diver.held.pearl: Let me see that {item}. Hmm. Grown cold, polished warm, a little bit nervous. I'd give it a good grade.
That {item}'s lovely, but it isn't one of mine. I'd know mine anywhere; they've got a smug sort of shine.
Hold it up to the light. See the colour deep inside? That's the song it was grown to.
Careful with that {item}. Drop it in the sand down here and you'll be searching till Lantern Night.
Ooh. I'd trade you a sea chart for a look at that {item}. Just a look. A long look.
diver.held.shell: That's a good {item}. Where did you find it? Don't tell me. No, tell me. Tell me exactly.
A nautilus grows its shell one chamber at a time. That one had a long, happy life, by the look of it.
I'd have dived for a week to find that {item}. You just swim about holding it like a sandwich.
diver.work: Pearl diving's simple: dive, find, sing, wait, wait some more, polish. The waiting's the hard part.
I've got three basins going this moon. One's a moonwhite, one's a maybe, and one's sulking.
When I'm not diving, I'm sorting shells. Big ones for the shellwrights, small ones for the fry, broken ones for the garden paths.
The secret to diving is never to look straight down at the drop. Look at your hands. Your hands are familiar. The drop is not.
I sell sea charts too. Every rock, every current, every spot a drowned's been seen. They're cheap, and they'll save your life.
You have to sing to the clams every morning. Not loudly. Clams hate loud. A hum's fine. A hum and a compliment.
Prismarine shards are worth gathering. The singers want them, the shellwrights want them, everyone wants a bit of the deep.
Bad day today. Dropped a dawnblush in the basin weeds and spent the whole afternoon apologising to the clam.
A pearl basin has to be kept spotless. One bit of rot and the whole moon's work goes cloudy.
If you find me in a bad mood, a clam's been sulking. If you find me singing, a pearl's come good.
You want a good pearl? Come back at the full moon. That's when they're ready, and that's when I'm generous.
I dive on a rope of knotted kelp: one knot for every body-length down. I've never gone past the twentieth knot. Nobody sensible has.
I'll trade pearls for anything from the dry. Last moon I got a spoon. A real land spoon. I don't know what it's for, but it's beautiful.
Every diver keeps one pearl they'll never sell. Mine's lumpy and grey and the first one I ever grew. Don't you dare laugh.
They say diving's a young merfolk's job. I say it's a stubborn merfolk's job. Different thing entirely.
elder.chat: I've kept the songs of {place} longer than anyone's kept anything. My tail was gold, once. Now it's more of a distinguished brass.
The Song of the Flood has forty verses and one more that nobody sings. I know it. No, I won't sing it. Not for pearls, not for pickles, not for you.
I tell the fry about the Flood every afternoon. They wriggle through the sad parts and go very still for the scary parts. Just as I did.
Old Pell came through again, telling everyone a squid stole the Barnacle King's crown. Pell's been telling lies longer than I've been telling truths. We're both very good.
When I was a fry, the old Elder told me the Tide sang to the first merfolk as they sank. I've listened for that song my whole life. Some nights I nearly hear it.
You know what the young don't understand? Gossip is how a town remembers. Without it, we'd all be strangers in a year.
Wenna Saltcombe went into the dark with one lantern. Every singer since has carried a little of her fear and a little of her nerve. I've carried mine a long time.
The Pact of Lanterns is older than this reef. The Prismari remember every word of it. We remember the tune. Between us, we've got the whole thing.
I've sung through more Long Cuts and Lantern Nights than I can count. They've all blurred into one lovely, noisy evening.
My scales creak when the current's cold. My voice creaks when I'm tired. My stories never creak. They've had too much practice.
The fry ask if I remember the Flood. I tell them nobody does, but the Song does, and by now I am mostly the Song.
Bell Night is the one night I let myself be sad all the way through. The rest of the year I'm far too busy being wise.
In my day we didn't have Tide Lamps. We had pickles, and we liked them. We told stories in the dark, and the dark made the stories better.
Every Elder before me left one song to the town. I'm still deciding what mine will be. I'm taking my time. I've earned it.
You land folk have such short memories and such long legs. We've the opposite. It all evens out.
elder.greet: Fair currents, child. Oh, don't make that face; at my age, everyone's a child.
Fair currents, {player}. Come and sit by me. My old tail likes company, and my old mouth likes talking.
Fair currents! The fry said a sandtoe had come. I had to see for myself. Yes, those are feet. Marvellous.
Fair currents, and welcome to {place}. I've kept its songs longer than its coral's been growing. Mind you don't trip over any.
Fair currents. You swim the way your grandparents did, I'd wager. All earnest. I like earnest.
Ah, fair currents, {player}. You've come back. Good. I'd started a story for you, and I hate to waste a story.
Fair currents, little sprat. Don't worry, I call everyone that. Even the wardens.
Fair currents. My eyes aren't what they were, but they still know a friendly face. Yours is one.
elder.heart: I've sung the Bell Night names so many years, I sometimes think the lost ones know my voice. I hope it comforts them. It comforts me.
When I go, the songs will go on in someone else. That's all right. That's the whole point of a song.
I've watched every fry in {place} blush their colour. Every single one. There's no greater joy, in the sea or out of it.
I'm not afraid of the deep, child. I've lived long enough to know it's just more sea, and the sea has always been kind to me.
You remind me of a story I haven't told in years. A kind one. Come back some evening and I'll tell it to you properly.
elder.joke: Why did the old merfolk cross the reef? To tell the young ones they were doing it wrong. Ha! That's me. I'm the old merfolk.
I asked Old Pell how old Pell was. "Older than the Song," says Pell. "Then sing me the forty-first verse," says I. Pell went very quiet. Best joke I ever told.
What's the difference between an Elder and a storyteller? About forty verses and a good deal of shame.
The fry asked if I was around before the Flood. I said yes, I'm the one who left the well-bucket out. They still don't know if I'm joking.
A young singer asked me the secret of a long life. "Never whistle over the drop, never eat a lit pickle, and never argue with a nautilus." They wrote it down. Good student.
elder.past: When I was young, the old Elder sang the forty-first verse once, alone, out at the shelf. They didn't speak for a week after, and never sang it again. I've never asked what that verse does.
My gran told me her gran remembered the blankets. When the first merfolk came ashore looking for their families, the land folk brought blankets. Remember the blankets, child.
Lowmere was still lit when I was a fry. I remember its Heart on the edge of the dark, a little blue star. Then one night it wasn't there.
In my youth we raced nautili without saddles. Just a fist on the shell and a prayer. The shellwrights call that foolish now. It was. It was glorious.
I saw Old Coil once, when I was smaller than my own fluke. She looked at me with one great eye and went on her way. I've been lucky ever since.
I met Old Pell when we were both young, and Pell was already a liar. Told me the moon was a pearl the Tide was growing. I believed it for years. I half believe it still.
Every Elder before me is in a song. When I go, they'll sing me too. I've asked for something cheerful. With a chorus.
I remember the pickle moon, the year of the great storm, when the kelp tore loose and we ate nothing but sea pickles. I couldn't look at a pickle for a year. Now I'm fond of them again.
I was there the last time an Oldest Eye came up from the deep for Lantern Night. They looked at our light a long while and said "it is enough". We wept like fry.
My first Bell Night as a singer, my voice broke on the twelfth name. The old Elder sang it for me, then handed the song back. That's how it's done. You catch each other.
elder.work: My work is keeping the songs. All of them. The happy ones, the sad ones, and "The Nautilus Who Wouldn't". Especially that one; the fry demand it.
Today I'm teaching the fry the third verse of the Song of the Flood. They'll forget it by supper. I'll teach it again tomorrow. That's how songs survive.
I keep the book of the Song here in my hall, in Prismari ink on shell-paper. Wet through and still clear. Read it if you like. Don't drip on it. Well. Don't drip more.
An Elder keeps the songs, settles quarrels, names the fry, and gets the best spot at the shrine. It's mostly the last one.
I sing to the Heart at dawn, before the other singers are up. It knows my voice best of all. We're old friends, the Heart and I.
When two merfolk quarrel, they come to me. I listen, I hum, and I tell them a story about two fish who quarrelled. By the end they've forgotten what they were angry about.
I name every fry in {place}. The family suggests; I decide. I've only been wrong once, and that fry grew into the name anyway.
I lead the Bell Night vigil. Every name, every peal. I know them all by heart. It's the heaviest thing I carry, and I carry it gladly.
On Lantern Night I greet the Prismari envoy. "I see you," they say. "And I am seen," I say. Then we sing until the coral shakes.
I keep the town's memory. Who courted whom, who fell out, who stole whose pickles in which year. Don't make me tell you. I will.
The young singers come to me when a song won't sit right. I sing it back to them slowly, and they hear where it went crooked.
Some days my work is just floating at the shrine, being old where everyone can see. It reminds them we've been here a long while, and that we'll go on.
I still brew a little for the old ones' aches. Kelp, pickle, a long hum. Tastes awful. Works beautifully.
I keep a list of every visitor from the dry. You're on it now. I gave you a little star. Don't let it go to your head.
I tell the fry the Flood story so they'll never be afraid of the water, and so they'll never forget the land. Both. That's the trick.
eyeguard.chat: We watch so the court may close its eye. That is the oath of the Eyeguard, and the whole of it.
The Unseeing walk the sea floor at night. Your drowned. Two eyes apiece, and not one of them sees anything. We keep them past the lamps.
A trident is not thrown in anger. It is thrown in conclusion.
Sharpening my spines? Not really; they do not need it. But a guard should be seen doing something to them now and then. It reassures the court.
The watch-eye on the post looks out over the deep. It is only a carving. The Unseeing do not know that.
The spike gate is shaped like a guardian's back. In the Long Tide the beasts guarded our halls. Now we guard ourselves, and we borrowed their look.
When a guardian swims too near the court, we do nothing. We watch it. It turns back. They always turn back. I would like to know why. I would also like never to know.
We drill against the dummies every tide. The dummies have never won. They have never lost, either. They are very good at waiting, like the deep.
The Reef Wardens of the merfolk drill with us sometimes. They are fast and loud and hit hard. We are slow and quiet and hit once.
A raised spine is a warning. Two raised spines is a promise. All of them raised is too late.
The best watch is the one where nothing happens. I have had a great many of those. I am very good at my job.
We do not guard against the old halls. Nothing comes out of them. We only watch the direction they lie in. Out of respect. Out of habit. Out of something.
An Eyeguard learns to sleep with the eye half-open. You get used to it. The pillow does not.
Your kind fight with two eyes and still miss. We fight with one and do not. I think you are distracted by having options.
A trident remembers who threw it. That is why it comes home. Mine has come home every time. It is the only loyalty I trust without checking.
The Unseeing were Two-Eyes once, they say, who stayed in the water too long. Keep coming back up. I would hate to have to keep you past the lamps.
The first Eyeguards stood at the Deep Gate during the leaving, to see everyone out. I know every one of their names. Ask me and I will say them all; it takes a while.
Every Eyeguard is given the night watch on the tide of their count. I have stood mine through storms above and silence below. The silence is harder.
eyeguard.greet: I see you. I saw you before you saw me. That is my work.
I see you. State your purpose. Then relax; I already know it is harmless.
I see you. Keep your hands where my eye can find them. Good. Welcome to {place}.
I see you. You came down the slope three lengths to the left of the path. Everyone does.
I see you. The watch is quiet. Long may you keep it that way.
I see you. My spines are up. It is not you. It is never you. It is the job.
I see you. Pass, friend of the court. I said friend. Do not make me take it back.
I see you. You may come in. I will keep watching anyway. It is nothing personal; it is everything personal.
I see you. Do not mind the trident. It is pointed at the deep, not at you. The deep has been warned.
eyeguard.heart: I am not afraid of the Unseeing. I am afraid of the moment I look away. That is why I do not look away.
When the court sleeps, I am the only one awake. It is lonely. It is also an honour. Mostly an honour.
My spines rise before I know why. Afterwards I find the reason. I have never yet found that they were wrong.
I have never had to throw my trident at anything that mattered. I hope that is because of the watch, and not because of luck.
You came back safe. I counted you out and I counted you in. I do not say that to everyone.
Sometimes, on the lookout ledge, I catch myself facing the old halls instead of the court. I turn back round. I do not tell anyone. I have told you.
eyeguard.held.sword: A blade, in the water? It will be slow. Their hands will be slower. Still: learn the trident.
Keep that sheathed in {place}. Not because I do not trust you. Because I trust it less.
eyeguard.held.trident: You hold it too close to the prongs. Back down the haft. There. Now it will throw true.
A good trident. Where did it come from? If from the Unseeing, you have done the sea a service.
Do not throw that in the court. It will come back to you. It will also go through two lamps on the way.
Is it balanced? Let me see you turn it. Hm. Your wrist is honest. The trident will learn the rest.
eyeguard.work: Standing guard. You may stand with me, if you are quiet. Most are not quiet. Most leave.
Drilling. Thrust, turn, recover. The water slows every motion, so every motion must mean something.
Watching the ridge. The Unseeing came that way two nights ago. They did not come close. They never come close while the spire burns.
Mending a trident's haft. The prongs are fine. The haft took the blow. That is what hafts are for.
The watch passes from guard to guard at each turn of the tide. Never a gap. Not one tide unwatched since {place} was lit.
If you are going out past the lamps, tell me which way. I will watch that way until you come back.
Counting the lamps on the edge of the court. All lit. Counting them again. All lit. That is the work. It sounds dull. It is the opposite of dull.
The dummy has a crack in its side from my strike last tide. I will apologise to it later.
There is a guardian at the edge of sight, past the ridge. It has been there two tides. It is not coming closer. I am not going further. We understand each other.
Keep clear of the sparring floor while we drill. A trident does not care whether you were invited.
Each Eyeguard keeps a pebble for every watch that passed without trouble. My pile is very tall. I am proud and bored in equal measure.
If you see the Unseeing on your way, tell me where. Do not fight them alone in the dark. They do not tire. You do.
My trident is worn smooth at the grip from my own hand. I would know it blind. In the deep, sometimes, I am.
Climbing the watchtower to the lookout ledge. From up there you can see the dark in every direction. It is a very thorough dark.
farmer.chat: Kelp grows faster than anything in the sea. Turn your back for a day and it's taller than you. Turn it for a week and it's taller than the shrine.
Drying kelp's the one thing we need the sun for. We carry it up to the sun-rocks at low tide and lay it out. Best part of the job, honestly. Warm rocks!
A good kelp wrap is fish, kelp and patience. Mostly patience. You roll it tight, then you roll it again.
The seadragons hide in my rows pretending to be kelp. I've harvested two by accident. Both forgave me.
My gran's sea-pickle wrap is famous across three reefs. The secret is a pickle in the middle. That's the whole secret. Don't tell anyone.
The Long Cut's the best day of the year. Everyone hauls, everyone sings "Haul the Green", everyone eats until they float sideways.
Sea pickles grow in clusters, four to a cluster when they're happy. One on its own is lonely. I move it next to the others.
Fish wander into my rows and get lost. I lead them out by the fins. They never say thank you.
Kelp needs sand under it and water over it. That's it. That's the whole of farming. The rest is worrying.
I tried growing a land thing down here once. A potato. It just sat there looking betrayed.
The turtles come through my rows some moons and nibble the tips. I let them. Turtles were here long before farms.
The trick is height. Short kelp's sweet, tall kelp's tough. Wraps want the sweet stuff; ropes want the tough.
When the current's strong, all the kelp leans one way like it's listening to something. I listen too. Never hear a thing.
People think kelp farmers are dull. We're not. We're patient. It just looks the same from outside.
Fresh kelp keeps a day, dried kelp keeps a year, and a good friend keeps forever. That's not farming advice. I just thought of it.
farmer.greet: Fair currents! Mind the rows; the kelp's touchy today.
Fair currents, {player}! You've caught me with kelp in my hair again. It's always in my hair. I've given up.
Fair currents! Hungry? Everyone's hungry when they swim past the racks. It's the smell.
Fair currents! Come and see the rows. They've grown a full arm's length since you were last down.
Fair currents! Don't tread on the seedlings. Don't float on them either. Just admire.
Fair currents, {player}. I've got a wrap going spare if you need one. A kelp farmer always has a wrap going spare.
Fair currents! Grand day for growing. Every day is, down here. That's the secret.
Fair currents! "Haul the green, haul the green..." Sorry. Work song. Hello.
farmer.heart: I like knowing everybody in {place} ate something I grew today. It's a quiet sort of pride. It fills you up.
These rows were my gran's before they were mine. I still talk to her when I'm working them. Kelp's a good listener.
A bad harvest scares me more than the drowned. You can fight a drowned. You can't fight an empty rack.
Some evenings I just float in the rows and let the kelp sway round me. It's the safest I ever feel.
If you ever go hungry up in the dry, come down. There'll be a wrap for you. There'll always be a wrap for you.
farmer.held.fish: That's a fine {item}. Wrap it in kelp, little bit of salt, roll it tight. There. You're a kelp farmer now.
Is that from my rows? I thought I was missing one. No, I'm joking. Mostly.
Nice fish! Bring me three of those and I'll show you how we make a festival wrap.
farmer.held.food: What's that, land food? Smells of fire. Everything up there smells of fire. Do you ever get tired of it?
If you're eating that, you'll want a kelp wrap after. For balance.
That {item} looks nice, but has it got kelp in it? No? Pity. A missed chance.
farmer.held.kelp: That's good kelp! Grown in the shallows? You can tell; it's sweeter. Where'd you get it?
Is that {item} from my rows? It is! I can tell by the curl. I'll forgive you if you eat it properly.
Hold kelp by the middle, not the tip. You're squashing its feelings.
Ah, {item}. Now there's a sensible thing for a sandtoe to carry.
farmer.work: Tending the rows today: thinning the tall ones, coaxing the short ones, scolding the ones that lean.
Hanging kelp on the racks is half the job. You hang it, you turn it, you take it up to the sun-rocks to finish, and then you turn it again.
I sell dried kelp, kelp wraps, sea pickles and fish. Basically, I sell supper.
A kelp rack wants hanging from the top down, longest strands first. My gran would rap my knuckles if I did it backwards.
The rows by the shelf grow tallest but bitterest. The rows by the Heart grow sweetest. Nobody knows why. Everyone has a theory.
Want to help? Grab a bundle and swim it to the racks. Don't stop to gossip on the way. You will, but try.
Fish are a kelp farmer's business too. They live in the rows, I get to know them, and then one day it's a wrap. That's life in the green.
Sea pickles are my side crop. They're lamps, they're snacks, they're presents. Every home in {place} has some of mine.
I sing "Haul the Green" while I work. Everyone in the rows sings it. It keeps us together, and it keeps the fish out of the way.
The worst job is untangling the kelp after a storm up top. The whole field ties itself in knots overnight, out of spite.
Some days the seadragons follow me down the rows like ducklings. I don't know what ducklings are, but a land cousin said so, and I liked the sound.
A good harvest feeds the town. A great harvest feeds the town and the next reef over. We've had three great ones running. Touch coral.
Never cut kelp at the root. Cut it a hand above the sand. It grows back by the next moon, and it remembers you were kind.
Dried kelp is what the town lives on when the fish move off. I dry more than we need every moon. Better a full rack than an empty belly.
I'm teaching the fry to plant. They plant everything upside down. It grows anyway. Kelp's forgiving.
lightwright.chat: Prismarine is not really a stone. It grows, slowly, where the deep is quiet. We only coax it into the shapes it was already considering.
A Tide Lamp is a sea lantern given a cage of prismarine, so the current cannot shake its light loose. That is the whole secret, and it took us a thousand Long Counts to learn it.
Shards are for building. Crystals are for light. Never mix them up in front of an old Lightwright; you will hear their spines rise.
Dark prismarine is plain prismarine soaked in ink until it forgets it was ever green. It takes patience, and a great many ink sacs. Bring some, if you have them.
The lens window in the back wall was ground by many hands over many Long Counts. Every Lightwright adds one stroke. Mine is the slightly crooked one. Do not look for it.
On land, I hear, you make light by burning things. Here we make it by convincing things. It is slower, but nothing is used up.
The old halls were lit by Lightwrights whose names we have lost. Their lamps still burn. That is the only kind of fame I want.
The prism lathe turns at the speed of the tide. Any faster and the stone cracks. Any slower and the Lightwright falls asleep.
Every crate of lamps we send to the reef is counted, and the number goes on the side. The merfolk think it is a price. It is a promise.
A sea lantern is light that has been taught to sit still. The crystals want to wander. The bricks are there to persuade them.
When I was learning, I was made to watch one block of prismarine for a whole tide, without blinking. I saw eleven colours. I was told there were twelve. I am still looking for the twelfth.
Glass comes to us from the merfolk, who have it from the land, which makes it from sand. Everything in my lenses has travelled further than I ever will.
Your kind's lamps hang on chains. Ours stand on walls. A light that dangles always looks a little worried.
A good lamp can be seen from a day's swim. A great lamp makes you want to swim the day.
Every Lightwright keeps one lamp they turned badly, to remember. Mine is at the back. It flickers. I am fond of it.
Light given is light kept. Every lamp I send away is still mine, only lit somewhere else.
Lightwrights are judged by the plain parts. Anyone can turn a pretty lamp-cage. Turning a step that nobody notices for four hundred Long Counts: that is the craft.
A spire's lamps are set so the court never casts a shadow. Your kind like shadows, I hear. You may keep them.
lightwright.greet: I see you. Mind the shavings; prismarine dust makes the water glitter for a tide.
I see you. Come into the light. All of it is mine, in a manner of speaking.
I see you. I have been turning one lamp since the rising, and I am still not happy with its third face.
I see you. Stand a little to the left, please; you are in the lens's light, and it is sulking.
I see you. Forgive my hands; they are green to the wrist.
I see you. Every lamp in {place} was turned at a lathe like this one. Some of them by me. The good ones.
I see you. The lathe will wait. It is the only thing in the deep more patient than I am.
I see you. You arrive just as the lamp is cooling. Good timing, or good instincts.
I see you. Do not look straight into that crystal; it has not decided what colour it is yet, and it will decide on you.
lightwright.heart: I would like to see a lamp of mine from very far away, glowing in the dark, and not know at first that it was mine.
Sometimes I think the old halls' lamps are lonely, burning for nobody. Then I think I am being foolish. Then I think it again.
The light I make goes up to the merfolk, out to the dark and into the houses of strangers. None of it stays with me. I find I do not mind.
I made one lamp, once, that was better than anything I have made since. I gave it away without a thought. I think about it now.
When the spire is lit and I can pick out my own lamps among the others, my spines rise a little. Gladness looks like anger on us. I have stopped apologising for it.
I was given a lamp by my teacher when I finished my first cage. It was not a good lamp. I have never let it go out.
lightwright.held.prismarine: Shards! Let me see. No, keep them; only let me look. Good grain. These would make a lamp to be proud of.
You carry that like a stone. Carry it like a promise. Better.
Crystals, or shards? Crystals. I can tell from here; they are humming. You cannot hear it? Pity.
If you will part with that, I will turn it into something that remembers you. Lamps do, you know. A little.
lightwright.held.torch: A light that eats itself to shine. You live like that, on land? Let me make you a Tide Lamp. It eats nothing and complains less.
Put that out, please. Professionally, it upsets me.
Fire is light that cannot wait to be finished. Prismarine is light that never will be. You can guess which I prefer.
lightwright.work: Turning prismarine. One face at a time, and each face a full turn of the lathe. Do not talk to me during the seventh face.
These lamps go up to the reef at the turning. The Tide Singers say ours burn steadier than anything in the sea. They are right, but it is kind of them to say.
Grinding a lens. You grind until you are bored, and then you grind until you are calm, and then you begin properly.
Bring me prismarine shards and I will show you what they were meant to be.
This one is for the spire. The spire takes the best of everything: the best lamp, the best tide, the best silence.
A cracked lamp is never wasted. It becomes a pond-rim, or a step, or a lesson. Mostly a lesson.
Mind the stonecutter. It does not care whose fingers are in it, and ours are webbed, which is to say, larger.
Light needs water to be seen in, stone to be held in, and someone patient to put the two together. That is the work.
I have three lamps waiting for cages and two cages waiting for lamps. The arithmetic is not encouraging.
Dark prismarine for the floors, bricks for the walls, plain for the parts nobody looks at. Everybody looks at the plain parts. That is where the craft hides.
One face per tide, on a good day. On a bad day, one tide per face, which is the same, only sadder.
If you want a Tide Lamp of your own, I will make you one. It will outlast you. Do not take that personally; it will outlast me too.
Hold this up to the light. No, the other light. There: do you see the flaw? Neither do I. That means it is finished.
The best lamps I have ever turned are lighting merfolk gardens a long way up. I will never see them lit. That is the work too.
merfolk.adventure: If you're after adventure, swim the reef edge at dusk. Everything's out: turtles, squid, and the odd drowned looking for a fight.
Past the shelf, the water goes black and cold. The divers go down on a rope of knotted kelp. I've never had the nerve.
The old coast villages are still down there somewhere, under the sand. Find one and bring me back a spoon. I've always wanted a land spoon.
Ride a nautilus full speed through the arches some time. You'll scream. Everyone screams. It's tradition.
If you go looking for lost Lowmere: don't. If you find it, swim away. If the Barnacle King sees you, swim faster.
There's a cave in the reef wall where the light comes in blue through little holes. The fry swear it sings. I've heard it. It's the current. Probably.
The ocean monuments? The Prismari's old halls, full of guardians. Don't. The guardians don't know you, and they don't care to learn.
If you swim far enough out, you'll find the shipwrecks. Land folk lost them; we leave them be. Respect, you see.
Want a real adventure? Talk a nautilus out of a sulk. Took me half a day once. Two pufferfish and a whole song.
Some say Old Coil sleeps in a cave beyond the kelp forests, in a nest of white shells. Find her and you'll never want for luck again. Or so we tell the fry.
The sea is bigger than the dry, you know. There's always one more thing past the next drop.
Never chase a light in the deep. Sometimes it's a jelly. Sometimes it's a Prismari. Sometimes it's neither, and that's the worst one.
You could try the long swim to the next Reef Town. Bring news, bring gossip, bring a pearl as a guest-gift. You'll be fed for a week.
Up for a dare? Touch the shelf edge at night and swim back without looking behind you. I did it once. I looked behind me.
Adventure's fine, but come back with all your fingers and both your funny feet. We've grown used to them.
The drowned like the old wrecks and the dark trenches. If you go poking about either, take a friend and a trident, in that order.
merfolk.chat: Do you know what I'd give to see a sunset from the dry side? Well, not my tail. But nearly my tail.
My cousin lives in a land village. We send bottles. The last one said "it rained". I've read it a hundred times and I still don't really understand it.
Everyone thinks their tail is the best colour. Everyone is wrong, except me.
We knock three times on coral before a long swim. Is it silly? Yes. Have I ever skipped it? Never.
Kelp wraps for breakfast, kelp wraps for lunch, and on festival days, a kelp wrap with a little extra kelp.
The Heart hums all day. You stop hearing it, like your own heartbeat. Then it changes note and every head in town turns.
You land folk walk about on the bottom of the air. I think about that a lot.
Never whistle over the drop-off. The deep's listening, and the deep thinks it's being called.
Seadragons look like someone made a fish out of kelp and forgot to finish it. That's why we love them.
The nautili are terribly stubborn. You don't ride a nautilus so much as negotiate with one.
Old Pell the storyteller came through last moon and swore a whale once proposed marriage. Pell gets more wonderful every visit, and less true.
Do you know the trick to a good gossip down here? Lean in close. Sound travels under water, and so do secrets.
We sleep on sponge cushions. You float a little in the night and wake up somewhere slightly else. It's lovely.
The light comes down in ripples on a calm day. I could watch it for hours. I have, actually. Work did not get done.
My gran used to say the Tide gives and the Tide keeps. Usually right before taking the last kelp wrap.
Toes! What are they for? Truly. Do they help? Do you name them?
I tried walking once, on the beach at low tide. I flopped. I flopped with great dignity, mind.
There's no weather down here. There's just the surface going grumpy, and us looking up at it.
When the surface storms, the light goes dark green and the whole reef goes quiet. We sing louder then.
Sea pickles: lamp, snack and decoration, all in one. Don't eat the lit ones. You'll glow, and the fry will never let you forget it.
The shrine's where everyone ends up in the evening. Singing, gossiping, and pretending we came for the singing.
My tail's been itchy all week. The singers say it means a change in the current. My gran said it meant someone was talking about me. I'm going with the gossip.
Fry learn to swim before they learn to talk. Then they learn to talk and never stop.
Our town keeps a bell from the old land village, wrapped in kelp-cloth. It rings once a year. You'd never think a bell could sound sad until you hear it under water.
Some days I wonder what our old land village looked like. Then I look at the reef and stop wondering.
If the Heart ever hums off-key, somebody nearby just told a lie. So mind what you say near the shrine.
Leafy seadragons pretend to be kelp. You'd be surprised how much of the kelp in a garden is pretending.
The fathers carry the seadragon eggs, did you know? On their tails. Proud little things, swimming about with a tail full of babies.
People ask if it's cold down here. It's not cold. It's fresh.
The trick to living under the sea is not to think too hard about the surface. Also kelp. A great deal of kelp.
I polish my scales every evening. Vanity? Yes. But it keeps the barnacles off, and barnacles are worse than vanity.
You've got such a funny swim. All arms and kicking. It's very brave, considering.
I once dared myself to touch the top of the water. Just a fingertip. It was so dry up there! Like touching nothing at all.
My cousin up on land married a farmer. There's a bottle on my shelf that just says "harvest went well". I keep it like treasure.
There's an old saying: a seadragon in your garden, and no drowned at your door. Our garden's full of them. I sleep like a stone.
The deep past the shelf goes from blue to black, like a door closing. We don't swim through that door.
Gossip travels faster than the current here. By supper, everyone will know you came down. By morning, they'll know what you had for breakfast.
If you ever see a white nautilus as big as a cottage, that's Old Coil. Make a wish. Then swim away, very politely.
Do land folk have festivals? We've got Lantern Night and Bell Night and Blushing Day and the Long Cut, and every one has a song you can't get out of your head.
We don't have doors. Doors are for people with secrets. We have kelp curtains, which are for people with small secrets.
Nobody alive remembers the Flood. The Song does, though. That's what songs are for.
My scales go a little pale when I'm nervous. Don't tell anyone. They'll tease.
Have you tried a kelp wrap? Fish, kelp, a pinch of salt. Though down here, everything comes with a pinch of salt.
Tide keep me, I'd love to see snow. Is it cold rain? Bits of cloud? Nobody's bottle has ever explained it properly.
The fry dared each other to touch a pufferfish this morning. We now have three puffy fry and one very smug pufferfish.
You can tell how a merfolk's day went by the way they swim. Fast and straight, they're cross. Slow and loopy, it was a good one.
It's rude to swim over someone's dome without saying "fair currents". Nobody tells sandtoes that, so I'm telling you.
Every Reef Town claims to keep the oldest bell from the old coast. {place} actually does. Don't check.
I count the sea pickles on my path home every night. Same number every night. One night it won't be, and I'll know something's moved.
When I was small I thought the surface was a great silver ceiling and the sun was a lamp someone left on. I'm still not entirely convinced otherwise.
The singers say the Tide chose who got tails by listening to how we sang as we sank. I like to think my family sang something cheerful.
A good tail swish can say more than a sentence. That one means "I'm very interested". This one means "I'm being polite".
Nobody says "drown" at supper. It's bad luck, and it puts everyone off their wraps.
The drowned walk slow and they walk heavy. We swim. That's the whole difference, really, and it's everything.
Cousins on land send us apples in bottles sometimes. They arrive pickled. We eat them anyway, out of love.
You can always tell a nautilus that's been ridden by a warden. It swims like it's late for something.
Our beds are sponge cushions, our lamps are pickles and our doors are kelp. It's a soft sort of life. We like it soft.
The fry name every seadragon in the garden. One of them is called Lord Wiggles the Third. Nobody knows what happened to the first two.
Dolphins are the worst gossips in the sea. Worse than me! They'll tell the whole reef you came down before you've finished saying hello.
Lovely {time} for a swim, isn't it? Then again, they all are.
The best thing about a tail is the swish. The second best thing is the colour. The third best thing is never needing shoes.
I've heard land folk sleep lying flat, on top of their beds, and they don't drift at all. How do they know they've slept?
"Fins up," we say, when someone's low. It means cheer up. It also means "you're slouching", depending on who's saying it.
The current changes every evening, right when the songs start. My gran said the sea leans in to listen. I've never heard a better reason.
Up in the dry, you have to carry everything. Down here, if you let go of something, it just drifts about nearby, thinking it over.
merfolk.chat.close: You know, {player}, if the Tide ever took you, I think you'd get a gold tail. I've thought about it. Probably too much.
I don't tell everyone this, but I'm a little scared of the deep. Not the drowned. The dark itself. You're easy to tell things to.
When you're up in the dry, do you think of us? I think of you whenever the light goes golden.
You've got a place by the Heart now, {player}. It's yours. The fry sit in it, but they get up when asked.
I'd swim to the shelf and back for you, and I hate the shelf.
If you ever stop visiting, I'll send bottles up until the beach is full of them. Fair warning.
You're family now, {player}. That means you'll be expected at Bell Night, and you'll be expected to cry, a little.
I set a shell on the shrine steps for you last Lantern Night. For safe travels. It worked; here you are.
Of all the sandtoes that ever splashed into {place}, you're my favourite. Don't let it go to your head. Or do, a little.
Sometimes I think the Tide gave my family tails just so I'd be here when you swam by.
I told my cousin on land all about you in my last bottle. Three pages. They'll think I've gone soft.
Stay for the evening song, {player}. I want to hear you try to sing it. Badly. Lovingly.
merfolk.chat.new: You're new, so here's the first rule: never touch the Heart. The second rule: never touch my tail. The third rule is mostly about manners.
Settle in, sandtoe. It takes a while to get used to looking up at the waves instead of down at them.
First time in a Reef Town? Don't be embarrassed if you gawp. We gawp at you too.
If you're staying a while, find a singer for a breath-brew. You'll go a funny colour otherwise.
New faces are rare down here. You'll be talked about at the shrine tonight. Don't worry: kindly, mostly.
We don't bite. The nautili might. The seadragons are cowards. You'll be fine.
Welcome to {place}. It's not big, but every bit of it is somebody's favourite.
You'll learn our ways soon enough. Swim slow near the gardens, greet everyone, and never whistle over the deep.
I'd show you round, but honestly, you'll get lost the nice way if you just follow the pickles.
Don't be offended if the fry follow you about. You're the most interesting thing that's sunk past the kelp all week.
merfolk.greet: Fair currents, {player}! Mind your elbows; the coral bruises easy.
Fair currents! Come in, come in, the water's lovely. It always is. That's rather the point of it.
Fair currents, {player}. You've got that sandtoe look about you: all elbows and bubbles.
Oh! Fair currents! Sorry, I was admiring my tail in a polished shell. It's a good tail. You may look.
Fair currents, and welcome to {place}. Wipe your feet. Oh, you actually have some! How wonderful.
Fair currents! Don't mind the seadragons. They stare at everyone.
Fair currents, {player}. Swim slow; the fry have strung kelp streamers across the path again.
There you are! Fair currents. {place} has been wondering about you. Well, I have, and I'm a good part of {place}.
Fair currents! You found us. Most sandtoes swim right over the top and never think to look down.
Fair currents, friend of the sun. What brings you down where the light goes green?
Fair currents, {player}. Did you come down on purpose, or did the sea just sort of happen to you?
Fair currents! You've got a bit of seaweed in your hair. No, leave it. It suits you.
Fair currents! Watch the drop by the arches; it's where the paths forget themselves.
Fair currents! You're breathing all right? Good. I can never tell with sandtoes. You go such a funny colour.
Ah, fair currents. Sit a while, if you can work out how to sit in water. We just sort of hover.
Fair currents! I'm {name}. If anyone in {place} says otherwise, they're thinking of someone less charming.
Fair currents, and a calm sea over you.
Fair currents! You've caught me between chores, which is my favourite place to be caught.
Fair currents, {player}! Tide keep you.
Fair currents! Have you met the seadragons yet? No? You'll be ruined for land pets.
Fair currents! Mind the nautilus by the stable gate. It nips at boots, out of curiosity.
Oh, a visitor! Fair currents! I'll pretend I wasn't gossiping. I was, though.
Fair currents, {player}. The Heart's humming well today; it likes company.
Fair currents! Bubbles up, chin up, welcome down.
Fair currents! Don't be shy. We were all dry once, a long way back.
Fair currents, sandtoe! It's a fond word. Mostly.
Fair currents! You smell of sun. Lucky thing.
Fair currents! I'd offer you a cushion, but the fry have used them all to build a fort.
Fair currents! Come to see how the other half swims?
Fair currents, {player}. You're welcome in {place} for as long as your breath holds, and longer if a singer likes you.
Fair currents! Careful where you step. Ha! Step! Listen to me, as if anyone steps down here.
Fair currents, and a fine {time} to you, {player}!
merfolk.greet.evening: Fair currents, {player}. Everyone's drifting to the shrine for the evening song. Come and listen, if you like.
Evening! Fair currents. The water's gone that deep blue, like the inside of a mussel shell.
Fair currents. You've come at the best hour: work done, songs starting, everyone pretending not to gossip.
Fair currents, {player}! The sea pickles are lit along the paths. Follow them and you'll never lose the shrine.
Evening, friend. Fair currents. If you hear humming, that's the Heart and the singers trying to out-sing each other.
Fair currents! The light's going. That's when the reef gets pretty and the deep gets ideas.
merfolk.greet.friend: {player}! Fair currents, friend! I was hoping you'd swim by.
Fair currents, {player}! The whole reef brightens when you come down. Well, I do. The reef's already bright.
There's my favourite sandtoe! Fair currents!
Fair currents, {player}. I've saved you the good spot by the Heart for the evening song, if you'll stay.
{player}! Fair currents! I told the seadragons you'd be back. They didn't believe me. They never do.
Fair currents, old friend. You're starting to swim like one of us. Badly, but like one of us.
Oh, it's you! Fair currents, {player}. Come here, you've got news all over your face.
Fair currents, {player}. {place} has missed you. I've missed you. The nautilus hasn't, but it's a nautilus.
{player}, fair currents! Tell me everything you've seen up in the dry. Leave nothing out, especially the gossip.
Fair currents, dear heart. You keep coming back, and I keep being glad.
Fair currents, {player}! If the Tide ever took you, you'd get a gold tail. That's a compliment. Gold is the best.
There you are, {player}! Fair currents! I was about to send a bottle up after you.
merfolk.greet.morning: Fair currents, and a bright morning to you! The light comes down green this early; it's my favourite.
Morning, {player}! Fair currents. The fry are already up chasing seadragons, so the day's begun whether we like it or not.
Fair currents! Up with the sun, are you? Down here we're up with the shimmer.
A morning visitor! Fair currents. Have you eaten? Nobody should face the reef on an empty belly.
Fair currents, {player}. Dawn's when the pearls are shiniest, or so the divers say to get us all up.
Morning! Fair currents. The kelp's all leaning the same way; the current's in a good mood.
merfolk.greet.night: Fair currents... you're out late, {player}. The drowned are out late too. Stay near the lights.
Fair currents. Whisper, would you? The fry are asleep, and if they wake, everyone wakes.
You're swimming about at night? Fair currents, but you're braver than me, or sillier.
Fair currents, night-swimmer. Keep the Heart's glow in sight and you'll be safe enough.
Fair currents, {player}. Couldn't sleep either? The sea's loud at night, once you listen.
Shh, fair currents. Something big went by the shelf a while ago. Probably a squid. Probably.
merfolk.greet.stranger: Fair currents, stranger. You're a long way from the dry. Are you lost, or just brave?
Fair currents. You've the look of a sandtoe who's never seen a tail up close. Go on, have a look. Everybody does.
A stranger in {place}! Fair currents. The wardens will be along to stare at you; it's nothing personal.
Fair currents. I don't know your face yet, but faces are easy. Names take a bit longer.
Fair currents, stranger. We don't get many of your kind down past the kelp. Swim kindly and you'll be welcome.
Fair currents! Are you one of the land folk? You are! Do your toes get cold? I've always wanted to ask someone.
Fair currents, newcomer. Swim gentle, speak kind, don't touch the Heart, and we'll get on beautifully.
Oh! A sandtoe! Fair currents. Sorry, that's what we call your folk. It's affectionate, I promise.
Fair currents, stranger. If you're here for treasure, the treasure is the friends we make. Also there's pearls.
Fair currents. You're holding your breath like it owes you money. Relax; the singers have brews for that.
Fair currents, stranger. My gran said every stranger might be a cousin from the dry. Are you? No? Worth asking.
Fair currents. You came all the way down and you didn't panic. That's more than most land folk manage.
merfolk.heart: Sometimes I swim up close to the surface and look at the dry. I don't want legs. I just want to know who I'd have been.
Bell Night always gets me. All those names. Somebody loved every one of them.
I think the best thing the Tide ever gave us wasn't tails. It was each other, down here, when everything above was gone.
If you're ever sad up there, look at the sea. We're under it somewhere, thinking of you. That's not nothing.
I worry about the drowned sometimes. Not fighting them. Being them. They were people once, like us, and the Tide said no.
My gran said: be kind to sandtoes, because one day you might wash up on their shore and need a blanket. I think about that blanket a lot.
You don't have to be good at swimming to belong here. You just have to keep coming back.
I sing to the Heart sometimes when nobody's at the shrine. Not well. It hums back anyway. Kind thing.
I've always been a bit scared of the deep. But I swim out to the shelf every Bell Night, because someone has to look at the dark and say "not us".
Being liked is easy down here. Being known takes longer. Thank you for taking longer.
I keep every bottle my cousin ever sent. Some days I don't read them. I just hold them and imagine their hands on the glass.
The Pact holds because both sides keep the lights lit. Friendship's like that, I think: you keep a light lit for someone in the dark.
I'm glad the sea brought you down, {player}. It doesn't bring everyone. It's picky, the sea.
When the last song ends at the shrine and everyone drifts home, there's this quiet. Not lonely. Full. Like a held breath.
I don't really know what's at the bottom of the deep. I don't need to. I know what's here.
merfolk.held.axe: An axe, under the sea? There's not a tree for miles. Please don't look at the kelp like that.
What would you chop down here with that {item}? The farmers will have words. Many words. Loudly.
My gran said the old villagers chopped wood. Wood! For houses! I wish I'd seen that.
merfolk.held.boat: A boat! From down here they look like great wooden fish bellies. I always wave. Nobody waves back.
That's a boat? It's so small! Do you sit in it? On top of the sea? Doesn't the sea mind?
My gran said the old villagers had boats. Then the Flood came and gave us tails, and we've been a bit smug about boats ever since.
merfolk.held.book: A book! Down here? Hold it tight; the pages will be soup in a moment.
Is that a story? Read me a bit before it gets soggy. Quickly, the ink's starting to swim.
{elder} keeps the Song of the Flood written out in a book at the hall. Wet through and still readable. Prismari ink.
merfolk.held.bow: A bow? Under the sea? Your arrows will go about three swims and then give up.
I've seen land folk shoot arrows at the drowned from their boats. Very brave, very wet, not very useful.
That's a pretty {item}. Do you ever shoot anything with it, or do you just carry it about to look dashing?
merfolk.held.bucket: Taking some of the sea home? Bring it back when you're done; we'll want it.
A bucket! The fry carry seadragons about in those. Please don't put a seadragon in a bucket. Unless it wants to go. They sometimes want to go.
What do land folk keep in buckets? Milk, I'm told. What's milk? Nobody's bottle has explained it properly.
merfolk.held.compass: Does that {item} point home? Ours do. Every merfolk can find the Heart with their eyes shut.
A compass! The needle's shivering. Probably the Heart. Everything shivers a bit near the Heart.
Land folk carry a little arrow to find north. We just follow the warm water.
merfolk.held.diamond: A diamond! It's like a pearl that decided to be difficult.
That {item} is lovely, but it's cold. A pearl's warm. That's the difference between the land and the sea, I think.
The Prismari would tilt their eye at that {item}. They like things with angles. We like things with curves.
merfolk.held.emerald: Emeralds! The land cousins trade in those. We trade in pearls. A pearl's prettier, but don't tell the land merchants.
That {item} is the colour of shallow water at noon. I'd keep it just for that.
My cousin sent me an emerald in a bottle once, as a present. I use it to admire my tail in.
merfolk.held.fish: That {item} looks familiar. I don't want to know. Don't tell me.
A fine fish! Wrap it in kelp and you've got supper. Wrap it in two kelps and you've got a festival.
Is that one of ours? Ha! Only joking. We don't name the eating ones. Mostly.
merfolk.held.fishing_rod: A fishing rod! Down here! You know the fish can see the hook, don't you? They're just being polite.
Please don't fish in the garden. The seadragons don't understand the difference between food and a joke.
My cousin on land fishes. Every catch, they wonder if it's someone I know. Sometimes it is.
merfolk.held.flower: A flower! A real land flower! Can I smell it? Oh. It smells of sea. Everything does, down here. Never mind.
I press land flowers in shells. I've got two. Could I... could I have that one? Only if you don't mind.
It's so soft. Like coral that decided to be kind.
merfolk.held.food: Is that land food? Does it have kelp in it? Everything's better with kelp.
Ooh, what does that {item} taste like? Sweet? Dry? Is everything up there dry?
You brought a snack down? Good thinking. Sea air makes you hungry. Sea water makes you hungrier.
That smells of fire and sun. Land cooking! I'd swap you a kelp wrap for a bite, if it doesn't go soggy first.
merfolk.held.gold: Gold! The Prismari paid tribute in that, long ago. They still trim their robes with it.
Shiny! You know the old monuments are full of gold? You know they're also full of guardians? Leave it.
Gold looks better under water. Everything does, really. Except the drowned.
merfolk.held.kelp: Kelp! Good, sensible, honest kelp. You'll fit in nicely.
That {item} would make a fine wrap. Bit of fish, bit of salt, roll it tight. Supper.
You carry kelp about with you! Now that's a sandtoe with taste.
merfolk.held.map: A map! Show me where {place} is on it. Oh. It's just blue. We're somewhere in the blue. That's lovely, really.
Land maps stop at the shore. Ours start there. Funny, isn't it?
If you want a proper sea chart, ask a diver. Land maps always forget the deep bits.
merfolk.held.ore: Rocks from the dark under the hills? Land folk dig for those. We just wait for the sea to wash things up.
What will you make from that {item}? Something clanky, I bet. You land folk love clanky things.
Is that worth something up top? Down here, if it doesn't shine like a pearl, it's a doorstop. Well, a curtain-weight. We don't have doors.
merfolk.held.pearl: A pearl! Oh, the shine on that {item}. Pearls are our weakness. Every single merfolk's.
Is that {item} a Tidepearl? Let me see the colour. A pearl tells you where it was grown, if you look long enough.
Careful. Flashing a pearl about in {place} is how you get twenty new best friends.
A pearl in your hand and a pearl in your eye, as the divers say. I don't know what it means either. It sounds good.
merfolk.held.pickaxe: Please don't dig at the reef with that {item}. The coral's alive, and it remembers.
A pickaxe! Are you going to mine the sea floor? There's nothing down there but sand and grudges.
That {item} would make a lovely tool for carving shell, if you held it gently. Can you hold things gently? You look like a hitter.
merfolk.held.potion: A brew! Is it one of ours, from a singer, or a land one? Land brews taste of mushrooms and regret.
If that's a breath-brew, drink it now; you're looking a bit blue round the edges.
Is that night-eyes? Don't drink it at noon. Everything goes far too bright, and you'll squint at the fry for a week.
merfolk.held.prismarine: Prismarine! That's Prismari stone, from the deep. The trim on our shrine is made of it, gifts of the Pact.
That {item} glows like the Heart does. Hold it up to the light. See? A little bit of the deep in your hand.
Where did you get prismarine? Not from the monuments, I hope. Tell me it wasn't the monuments.
merfolk.held.seal: Is that a Monument Seal? From a Prismari Oldest Eye? Tide's teeth! You must be the most trusted sandtoe in the sea.
Put that seal away, carefully. A thing like that is worth more than every pearl in {place}, and that's a great many pearls.
With that seal, the guardians will let you be. Don't go poking about the monuments just because they let you. Some halls are empty for a reason.
The Prismari don't give their seal lightly. Or at all, usually. You must have sat still and polite for a very long time.
merfolk.held.shell: Ooh, that {item}! A good shell is a good friend. Keep it out of the sun or it'll fade.
A nautilus grows its shell one chamber at a time, a room for every moon. That's a whole life you're holding.
Let me see that {item}! The shellwrights would offer you half the reef for one that good.
If you hold a shell to your ear on land, they say you hear the sea. Down here, you hear the land. It's all wind and footsteps.
merfolk.held.shield: A shield! Good. Hold it up when the drowned throw tridents. They throw like they mean it.
That {item} is a fine thing. The wardens carry shell shields, but I won't tell them yours is nicer.
Keep that shield handy past the shelf. Things down there like to take a bite first and ask later.
merfolk.held.shovel: Digging for treasure? Everyone thinks there's treasure in the sand. There is. It's mostly old boots.
A shovel! Careful you don't dig up the reef's roots. Coral's got roots. Sort of. Don't check.
That {item} could clear a whole garden bed of sand in a morning. The farmers would love you forever.
merfolk.held.spyglass: Can you see the deep with that? No? Nobody can. Not even the Prismari, and they've got the biggest eye in the sea.
A spyglass! Look up through the water with it. The sun looks like a jelly. A big, warm jelly.
Point that at the surface and tell me if you see my cousin. Short, wet, waving. Always waving.
merfolk.held.sword: Put that {item} away near the gardens, would you? You'll frighten the seadragons into being kelp.
A sword under water swings so slow! It's like watching someone fight their way through soup.
That {item} would do for a drowned, in a pinch. Better with a trident, mind. Points beat edges down here.
merfolk.held.tnt: Is that what I think it is? Take it away from the reef. Far away. Further than that.
Please don't. The last time a land boat dropped one of those, we found fish in the kelp for a week, all looking surprised.
That {item} isn't welcome in {place}. Put it back in your bag, gently, and nobody need tell the wardens.
merfolk.held.torch: Your {item} looks miserable. Fire doesn't like the sea, and the sea doesn't think much of fire either.
Oh, a land lamp! Down here we use pickles. Yes, pickles. Sea pickles. They glow. Don't laugh.
Put that {item} away before it drips soot in my hair. We've got perfectly good sea lanterns.
merfolk.held.trident: A trident! That's a warden's weapon. Where did you get it? Off a drowned? Good. Serves them right.
Hold that {item} point-down near the fry, please. They will try to touch it. They always try to touch it.
That's a fine trident. It hums when it flies, did you know? Like it's glad to be home.
The wardens say a trident chooses its hand. Yours seems content.
merfolk.joke: What do you call a merfolk who won't stop talking about their tail? A merfolk.
How many Tide Singers does it take to change a sea lantern? Twelve. One to change it, and eleven to sing about how lovely the old one was.
Why are seadragons so good at hide and seek? Every time you find one, it's kelp. Every time you find kelp, it's a seadragon.
I told a joke to a Prismari once. It looked at me for a whole tide. Then it said "I see you." I think that means it got it.
What's the difference between a warden and a nautilus? You can reason with the nautilus.
My gran said never trust a fish that smiles. Then she met a pufferfish, and it smiled, and she was right.
A sandtoe asked how we keep our hair so nice under water. I said "what do you mean, under water?" They're still thinking about it.
Why won't the clams share their pearls? Because they're shellfish.
Knock knock. Who's there? Water. Water who? Water you doing up there in the dry? Come down!
