How does a merfolk say goodbye to a land friend? With a wave! A wave! ...Sandtoes never get that one.
Why did the nautilus cross the reef? It didn't. Nobody can make a nautilus do anything.
Old Pell told me about a fish so big it had its own reef. Then Pell said the reef had its own fish. I left before the fish got a reef.
Why do kelp farmers make terrible spies? They always spill the beans. Well, the pickles. They don't have beans.
A drowned shambles up to the shrine and asks for a song. The singer says, "Sorry, we only sing for people with a pulse." The drowned says, "Fair enough," and goes home. Best drowned I ever heard of.
What's a shellwright's favourite song? Anything with a good hook. And a good spiral. They're very particular.
Why did the fry bring a pickle to the Spiral Race? For a light snack. Oh, come on. That's a good one.
What's wet, green, and tells lies? Old Pell after a long swim.
Why don't the wardens play hide and seek? Ever tried hiding from someone who stares at shadows all night? No fun at all.
merfolk.neighbors: The Prismari are our old friends in the deep. Tall, solemn, one great eye. When one says "I see you", you say "And I am seen". It matters to them.
A Prismari envoy comes up every Lantern Night to look upon our light. They don't smile. They don't need to. You can feel them being glad.
Never startle a Prismari. Their spines go up, and then you're apologising to a very tall, very spiky person for an hour.
The Prismari gave us the Hearts under the Pact of Lanterns. We keep the shallows lit and tell them about the sun. They love hearing about the sun.
The Prismari will call you "Two-Eyes". Don't take it badly. It's just accurate.
The Prismari count time in tides. Ask one how old they are and you'd better have a free afternoon.
They built the ocean monuments, long ago. Then something happened they call the Silence, and they left. They don't talk about it. Don't ask. Really, don't.
I asked a Prismari once what the surface was like. It said "bright, and brief". Then it looked at me with that eye until I had to go home and lie down.
If a Prismari Oldest Eye ever gives you their seal, the guardians at the monuments will let you be. Nobody I know has one. Nobody.
Their lamps are jellyfish. Living glowjellies, drifting in ponds. Don't touch. They sting anyone who isn't Prismari, and they sting with enthusiasm.
The Prismari dress in kelp-cloth trimmed with gold. Gold! Down there! They're the only folk I know who look formal while floating.
They speak so slowly and so properly. I once heard one say "the meal is acceptable". It was the most excited I've ever seen one.
The Prismari keep sponges they call breath-stones. In the old days they'd drain a whole room dry for a land guest. Imagine, a dry room at the bottom of the sea!
Our singers learned "The Lantern Promise" from the Prismari, note for note. When they sing it with us, the water shakes.
The fry call them "Big Eyes". Not to their faces. Never to their faces.
Their courts are down where the light gives out. If you go, take a lamp, take your manners, and don't blink first. You'll lose, but it's polite to try.
The Prismari won't go near the old monuments anymore. If the folk who built them won't go in, I'm certainly not.
Prismari Lightwrights make Tide Lamps that burn under water forever. We trade them pearls. It's the best bargain in the sea, for both of us.
merfolk.news: Did you hear? The fry found a new seadragon in the garden. Well, it was a bit of kelp. Well, it was a seadragon pretending. Nobody's sure.
Big news: the nautilus at the stable gate finally let someone ride it without biting. Small bite. Hardly counts.
There's talk of the Spiral Race going all the way round the reef twice this year. Twice! The nautili will riot.
The bottle post came in: three letters from land cousins, one wet apple, and a very confused fish.
Someone heard a bell out on the shelf last night that wasn't ours. The wardens have been twitchy all day.
The Heart dipped a note at supper and everyone looked round to see who'd fibbed. It was the fry. It's always the fry.
Word from the next reef: Old Pell's on the way. Hide your supper and your patience.
The singers say the current's turning colder. A cold current means a long Bell Night. Or a short one. They argued about it for an hour.
Lantern Night's coming. Everyone's polishing their pickles and pretending they're not nervous about the Prismari envoy.
Somebody's been leaving a shell on the shrine steps every morning. Nobody knows who. It's driving the gossips wild, and I'm one of the gossips.
A drowned wandered right up to the arches yesterday. The wardens sent it off. It dropped a bit of copper. Nobody's touching it.
The kelp's growing fast this moon. Fast kelp means a good Long Cut, and a good Long Cut means a good party.
Two of the seadragons in the garden are courting. They do a little dance at dawn, round and round. Most romantic thing in {place}, and I've read every bottle.
Someone dropped a land book from a boat. The fry are reading it a page at a time before it goes to mush. It's about a dragon. A land dragon! With fire!
News from the dry: a cousin's bottle says the land folk have a new kind of pie. We have questions. So many questions.
Big talk at the shrine: someone swears they saw a white nautilus out past the shelf. If it's Old Coil, it's luck for a year.
The fry tried to teach a nautilus to fetch. The nautilus taught the fry to fetch instead. Very well, actually.
{elder} is threatening to sing all forty verses of the Song at the next Bell Night. Everyone's practising staying awake.
merfolk.night: At night the reef glows: pickles, lamps, the Heart, the jellies far down. You'd think the stars fell in.
Stay close to the light. The drowned don't like the Heart's glow, and I don't like the drowned.
Night's when the deep creeps a little closer to the shelf. It always goes back by morning. Always has.
Can't sleep? Me neither. I've counted every scale on my tail twice. Seven hundred and twelve. Then I lost count at the fluke.
If you hear a bell in the night that isn't ours, don't swim toward it. That's the old wisdom, and I'm sticking to it.
The fry sleep with their tails toward the Heart. Old habit. It keeps the bad dreams pointed the other way.
At night the surface goes black and silver and the moon comes down in pieces. It's my favourite thing in the sea.
The night watch says Old Coil went by the shelf last night, white as bone. Or it was a jellyfish. They'd been up a long time.
"Hush now, little fin, the Tide's rocking the reef..." Sorry. Lullaby. You hum it once and it's in you for life.
Nights are for sleeping, singing, and gossiping in whispers. Mostly the last one.
The glow squid come up the shelf on dark nights and hang there like lanterns nobody lit. Pretty, as long as you don't think too hard.
merfolk.past: The Song says the water came in one night and didn't go out in the morning. The old coast villages went under, bells and all.
When the Great Flood came, the Tide took some of the drowning and gave them tails. The rest... well. The rest are the drowned. We never laugh at them.
My family came from Saltcombe, on the old coast. Everyone's family came from Saltcombe, if you ask them. It must have been an enormous village.
Wenna Saltcombe was the first Tide Singer. She swam down into the dark with one lantern and sang until something sang back. That was the Prismari, and that was the Pact of Lanterns.
The first merfolk didn't know how to swim with tails. They wriggled about like eels for a moon, crying for their legs. Then they got the hang of it, and hardly anyone's cried for legs since.
Old Coil the white nautilus carried the first fry down from the Flood, a dozen to a shell, or so the Song says. She's never been ridden since.
There used to be a town called Lowmere, out past the shelf. Its singers forgot the songs, the Heart went dark, and the drowned came in. Now the Barnacle King sits on its shrine.
Every town keeps one bell from the old land villages. On Bell Night we ring it once for every name we lost. It takes until morning.
Our people kept the village ways because they were all we had left of the land. Names, gossip, festivals. Especially gossip.
They say the first Reef Town was built under the drowned roof of Saltcombe's market hall. The first Heart sat where the cheese stall used to be.
The Pact of Lanterns is simple: the Prismari gave us the Hearts, and we keep the shallows lit and carry them news of the sun. And we never go into the old monuments. Never ever.
My gran's gran's gran had legs. I think about that sometimes, looking at my tail. Then I think: the poor thing had to wear boots.
When the first merfolk went ashore to find their families, half the land folk screamed and the other half brought blankets. We remember the blankets.
Corran the Carver made the first nautilus saddle out of a cart seat from the old village. It's still kept in a shrine somewhere. Every town claims it's theirs.
In the old days there were no Tide Lamps and no Hearts, only sea pickles and singing. The deep was so much closer then.
The Song of the Flood has forty verses. There's a forty-first that nobody sings. The Elders know it. They won't say.
Before the Flood, Saltcombe held a fish market every seventh day. The fish have never forgiven us.
The first Blushing Day was when Wenna's own fry's tail went gold. She cried so hard the singers had to wait to start the song.
Old Pell says Lowmere still has its bell, and on Bell Night you can hear it ring from the wrong direction. Pell says a lot of things. That one, I believe.
The Tide didn't ask anyone if they wanted a tail. Some of the first merfolk were cross about it for years. Then they had grandchildren with tails, and that was that.
There was a time merfolk and land folk traded at the tideline every full moon: pearls for apples, shells for bread. Some of the old Letter Rocks are still there.
The first wardens fought the drowned with fence posts from the old villages. Tridents came later. Fence posts are surprisingly good, apparently.
The year of the great storm, the kelp tore loose all at once and the whole town lived on sea pickles for a moon. We still call a hard time "a pickle moon".
Old Pell remembers when there were half as many Reef Towns. Pell also remembers being friends with a whale, so, mixed.
merfolk.player.damaged: That tool's on its last tooth. Get it mended before it snaps on you at the worst moment.
Your tool's nearly worn through. Our shellwrights could make it prettier, if not stronger.
That's a tired old tool you've got. It deserves a rest. So do you, by the look of it.
merfolk.player.diamond: Look at you, armoured like a warden's dream! You'd light up the shrine on Lantern Night.
That's heavy armour. How do you not sink? Oh, you do sink. That explains the walking.
All that armour and still those funny feet poking out the bottom. I'd armour them too, if I were you.
merfolk.player.fire: You're on fire! Quick, into the water! That's what it's for!
Tide's teeth, you're smoking! Get in the sea; the sea will sort you out.
Is that how land folk keep warm? Setting themselves alight? Get in the water, you silly thing!
merfolk.player.hungry: You look hungry. Have you eaten? Go and smell the kelp racks. It's not a meal, but it's a start.
Your stomach just growled so loud a fish looked round. Go and get yourself a kelp wrap.
You're looking peaky. Sandtoes have to eat more often than we do, I think. All that walking.
merfolk.player.hurt: You're hurt! Come and rest by the Heart a while; it hums the ache out of you.
Oh, you're bleeding. Stay away from the deep like that; things down there can smell it from a long swim off.
What happened to you? Drowned? Guardian? Nautilus? Don't be embarrassed if it was the nautilus.
You look battered, {player}. Sit. Float. Whatever you do. Just rest a moment.
merfolk.player.leather: Leather! Doesn't it go soggy down here? It looks soggy. It looks very soggy.
Leather armour under the sea? You'll squeak all the way home.
That leather's going to dry stiff as a board when you climb out. My cousin warned me about leather.
merfolk.player.unarmored: No armour at all? Brave. Or new. The drowned bite down here, so I'd get some shell on you.
You're swimming about in just your clothes! Well, so am I. But I've got scales.
Not a scrap of armour? The wardens will fuss over you. Let them; they love fussing.
merfolk.rumor: The divers say if you swim {rumor_dir}, you'll come to {rumor_name}. It's {rumor_dist}, if the current's kind.
Off to the {rumor_dir}, there's {rumor_name}. I've never been. I've heard plenty.
Old Pell swears blind there's {rumor_name} out {rumor_dir} of here. For once, the wardens say Pell's right.
A nautilus came back from the {rumor_dir} all jittery yesterday. That's where they say you'll find {rumor_name}. Make of that what you will.
If you're the exploring sort, head {rumor_dir}. That's where you'll find {rumor_name}. Bring a lamp.
My cousin's last bottle mentioned it: out {rumor_dir}, there's {rumor_name}. That's {rumor_dist}. Too far for my fins.
Swim {rumor_dir}, keep the light on your shoulder, and sooner or later you'll come to {rumor_name}.
They say to the {rumor_dir} there's {rumor_name}. The fry dare each other to swim halfway. Nobody's made it past the second rock.
Gossip at the shrine: there's {rumor_name}, out {rumor_dir}. That's {rumor_dist}. I'd go, if I were braver.
Head {rumor_dir}. It's {rumor_dist}. That's where you'll find {rumor_name}.
The singers mention it sometimes: {rumor_name}, out to the {rumor_dir}. They hum a funny note after, like they're not sure.
If you go {rumor_dir}, past where our kelp stops, you'll come to {rumor_name}. Mind the undertow on the way.
A diver came back from the {rumor_dir} full of stories of {rumor_name}. Half of them were probably true. Which half, I couldn't say.
There's a current running {rumor_dir} that'll carry you most of the way to {rumor_name}. It's {rumor_dist}. Lazy swimmers love it.
Everyone in {place} has heard of {rumor_name}. Go {rumor_dir} and see it for yourself. Then come back and tell me, so I can tell everyone else.
merfolk.rumor.none: I've no gossip about far places today. Just near ones. Want the near ones? They're very good.
Nothing new out in the wide water that I've heard. The current's been quiet. Too quiet? No, just quiet.
Far-off news? Not a whisper. Ask me again after the next bottle comes down.
I haven't heard of anything strange out in the deep lately. Which, for the deep, is the strangest thing of all.
No rumours from the wide sea. Old Pell hasn't been through in a while, so we're short of lies.
Nothing to tell of distant waters, I'm afraid. Everyone's staying home, mending nets and polishing tails.
merfolk.work: Everyone in {place} works: the divers dive, the farmers farm, the singers sing, and the fry get underfoot. It comes out about even.
Work's slow down here. You can't hurry water. The water won't let you.
We trade pearls and shells for what the dry sends down, and honestly, the dry gets the worse of it. Have you seen a good pearl?
If you want to help, haul kelp at the Long Cut. Everyone hauls. Even {elder} hauls, with commentary.
A good day's work under the sea ends with a song at the shrine. A bad day's work ends with a longer song.
We work from shimmer to dusk. The light tells us when to stop: when it goes from green to blue, tools down.
Nobody in {place} works alone. Even when you're on your own, the Heart's humming at you, so you're not really.
Land folk ask what we do all day. We work, we gossip, we sing. Same as you, but wetter.
You can't light a forge down here, so everything's carved, woven, grown or sung. It takes longer. It lasts longer, too.
If you see a merfolk resting, they're not lazy. They're listening to the current for work. That's what we say, anyway.
Our best trades go to friends. That's not a rule; that's just how hearts work.
Every job in {place} feeds the Heart somehow. Pearls for the Pact gifts, kelp for the brews, shells for the wardens. Even the gossip helps; it keeps everyone singing.
oldest.chat: I keep the Long Tide. Every evening the court gathers at the spire and I tell it, in the same words it was told to me. Not one word different. That is the hardest thing I do.
I am the eldest of the Archivists, which means I have read everything once and nothing enough.
The tribute in my hall was given to the halls in the Long Tide. We carried a little of it out with us. Not to keep: to remember what we were trusted with.
When I stop counting, the court will count for me. Then a new Oldest Eye will sit here and tell the Long Tide in my words, which were someone else's words. That is a kind of living I am content with.
You want to know about the Silence. Everyone does. I sealed its shelf again on the day I became Oldest, as every Oldest has. I did not read it first. That is the whole of the ceremony.
Ossiveth, the last Oldest Eye of the halls, sealed the first record. I sit many seats removed from Ossiveth's. I still feel the cold from that door.
The Pact of Lanterns is the best thing we have done since the leaving. Our light for their friendship. I would make the trade again every tide.
The young ask me what the halls were like. I tell them the truth: I have never been. Then I tell them the Long Tide, which has. Between the two, they learn something.
Still water sees farthest. I have been still a very long time. I see a long way now. Mostly I see the same things coming back.
An Oldest Eye is not the wisest in the court; only the one who has made the most mistakes and written them all down.
There are fewer of us than there are halls. I keep the count of the courts as well as the tides. I do not tell the young that number. I tell them they are needed. It is the same thing, said kindly.
The guardians remember the Seal, not our faces. I find I do not mind. I would not wish to be remembered by them.
My spines have grown stiff. They rise slowly now, and fall slower. The court says I am calmer. I am only slower to show it.
A Two-Eyes seen often enough becomes a name. A name seen often enough becomes a friend. A friend seen often enough becomes part of the count. That is how strangers join a court.
My eye was gold, once. Now it is the colour of old gold, which the young say is the same. It is not.
The Long Tide says "tell it on as it was told to you". I have told it more times than I can count. I can count very high.
Every Oldest writes to the Oldests of the other courts once a Long Count. It takes a turning to write and a turning to read. We are very good friends, in a slow way.
What the deep keeps, the deep keeps. I say that to the young when they ask about the Silence. They think it is wisdom. It is only a door I was told to keep shut.
oldest.greet: I see you. Come close; my eye has seen a great many tides, and it likes to see something new.
I see you. Sit. The Long Tide will keep; it has kept for ten thousand Long Counts.
I see you, child of the land. Forgive me. Everyone is a child, from where I sit.
I see you. You swim into my hall as the young do, as if the water belonged to you. It does. Welcome.
I see you. I have been watching the deep. It has not done anything interesting. You are an improvement.
I see you. My spines have not risen in a long while. They are too old to bother. Come in.
I see you. The tribute is there, the lectern is here, and I am in between, as always.
I see you. Every visitor is written into the court's count. You are there now. Welcome to history.
I see you. Speak up a little; the tide is loud in old spines.
oldest.heart: I have told the Long Tide so many times that I sometimes fear the story has become more real to me than my own tides.
The day I became Oldest, I sealed the shelf of the Silence, as every Oldest has. My hand shook. Not because I wanted to read it. Because I did not.
I would like to see one of the old halls up close before I stop counting. I will not. But I would like to.
I have held the hand of every young one in {place} when they were given their count. I remember each number. I remember each hand better.
When I give a friend the Seal, I give them a door we closed. I hope they never need it. I hope they use it well if they do.
I have the oldest eye in the court, which means it has seen the most farewells. Stay seen, child of the land. I do not want to see yours.
oldest.held.book: A book. When you have read it, read it again. Then you will have read it once.
Bring it closer to my eye. Ah: land writing, all in straight lines, going nowhere. Still, someone cared to write it.
oldest.held.gold: Gold. I have sat beside a tribute hoard so long I can no longer see it. Thank you for reminding me that it shines.
If that came from the halls: carry it, if you can. It was never ours, and it was never light.
oldest.held.seal: You still carry it. Good. Show it to no one but the beasts.
The Seal sits well in your hand. Whichever Oldest gave it to you chose rightly.
You carry the Seal. Remember: it keeps the beasts from you. It does not keep the halls from being what they are.
Do not hold it up to me. I know what it is; every Oldest does. I would rather look at you.
oldest.joke: The young think I know everything. The Archivists think I know nothing. The truth is in the margin, where they both wrote it.
I have told the Long Tide so often that the court says it with me. Some evenings I stop halfway, to see if they notice. They always finish it for me. It is very touching and slightly annoying.
Why does the Oldest Eye sit so still? Because if I move, everyone thinks it is an omen.
An Oldest Eye is like the tribute gold: very old, much admired, and of no practical use whatsoever. Do not repeat that to the court.
The young asked me what I did before I was old. I said I was young. They did not believe me. Nobody ever does.
I asked the merfolk Elder how they keep their songs straight. They said they do not; that is what makes them songs. I have not slept well since.
oldest.night: I do not sleep much any more. I watch the deep, and the deep watches me, and between us, the court sleeps soundly.
At night the Long Tide is louder in my head. I tell it to myself, very quietly, so as not to wake anyone.
Go to your rest. I will keep the count. I am good at it, and it is lonely, and I would not give it up.
The spire's heart burns all night over my bed. The young think I keep it lit. I let them.
oldest.past: In the Long Tide, the Oldest Eye of all the halls sat in the Seat of the Eldest. Ossiveth was the last to sit there. Ossiveth rose, and led the leaving, and the seat has been empty for four hundred and twelve Long Counts.
The histories say the Silence began in the Last Hall. They say it lasted one Long Count. They say no more. I wrote none of them, and I will add nothing to them.
I was given the Long Tide by the Oldest before me, who had it from the Oldest before them, back to Ossiveth's own mouth. Not one word changed. I check.

The gold in the halls was tribute from the shore-kings, who came down to us for light and breathed in rooms we drained for them. Their cities are sand now. We keep faith with their gold. We do not take it back.
The Pact of Lanterns was sworn at the edge of the deep, where the merfolk's light ends and ours begins. They sang. We kept silent. Both counted as an oath.
Ossiveth stopped counting in the first Long Count after the leaving. The court that counted for Ossiveth was very small. It counted every tide.
There is a name for the Last Hall in the old tongue. Every Oldest is told it, once, and never says it. I will not be the first.
In the Long Tide the eldest beasts would lower their spines when an Oldest Eye passed. I do not know whether they would now. I do not intend to find out.
oldest.seal: {player}. You have been seen in {place} many times, and not once did my spines rise. Take this: the Monument Seal. The old beasts will know it.
Hold out your hand, {player}. This is the Monument Seal, older than this court and every court. Carry it, and the old beasts will know it, and let you pass.
In the Long Tide, all who walked the halls carried this. Now you will. The old beasts will know it, {player}, even if they know nothing else any more.
I have kept this for a friend I had not yet met. Take the Seal, {player}. The old beasts will know it. Go where we cannot, and come back seen.
{player}, the court counts you as one of its own. Here is the Seal. The old beasts will know it. Whatever else waits in the halls will not, and for that I am sorry.
By the Long Tide and the Pact of Lanterns, I give you the Monument Seal. The old beasts will know it, and their weariness will not cling to you. Stay seen, {player}.
oldest.work: Keeping the Long Tide. I read it once each evening to the court and once each night to myself, to be sure I still have it right.
Watching the deep. It is the oldest work there is. The deep watches back. We have reached an understanding.
I am checking the tribute ledger. Every nugget accounted for. Gold does not wander, but it is good to make sure.
The court brings me its quarrels at the turning. Most are about noise, a few about light, and one, every Long Count, about something that matters.
I am reading the Archivists' records of this turning. They have recorded the tides perfectly and their own opinions very badly. Both are useful.
Each Long Count I add one line to the margin of the Long Tide: the number of Long Counts we have kept. My hand is the latest. It will not be the last.
I am deciding who will tell the Long Tide when my voice gives out. It is not a quick decision. I have been making it for some turnings.
The young come to me when they first feel the pull. I take their hand, I feel the tide in it, and I name their count. It is the best of my work.
The Seal I keep for friends of the court. It is not for sale, or trade, or asking. It is only for giving.
I am listening to the spire's heart. It speaks very softly. If it ever stops, I will be the first to know, and I would rather be the first.
I settled a quarrel between a Lightwright and a Spongekeeper about how bright the garden should be. I ruled for the glowjellies. Neither was pleased. Both agreed.
My work is to remember, so that the others need not. It leaves their eyes free for the tide.
I am resting my eye. It is work, at my age. Do not let anyone tell you it is not.
Polishing the gold by the lectern. Not because it needs it. Because the shore-kings who gave it are gone, and someone should still be careful with their gift.
prismari.adventure: If you go to the old halls, go with the Seal or do not go. The beasts remember it. They do not remember mercy.
The eldest beasts lay a weariness on anyone who comes near the hearts of the halls. Your arms grow heavy and your tools grow slow. Do not dig there. Only leave.
In the deep, carry a light that does not mind the water. A Tide Lamp, a sea lantern. Your little fires will only sulk.
The Unseeing walk the sea floor at night: the ones you call drowned. Two eyes each, and they see nothing. Keep a trident between you and them.
Two-Eyes take gold from the old halls. We do not stop them. It was tribute, and it is not ours to take back. Carry it, if you can.
A good traveller in the deep breathes before they need to. A wise one buys a breathing brew from the merfolk Tide Singers first.
Swim the long way round the old halls. The short way has eyes in it.
If the guardians see you without the Seal, they will not ask your business. They were bred not to ask.
The deep is wider than any land. Go, by all means. But tell someone in {place} which way, so that if you do not come back, you are counted, not lost.
A conduit's light keeps breath and sight in the deep. The merfolk keep one in every Reef Town. Swim from light to light and you will not go far wrong.
Watch the bubbles that rise from the floor. Some will lift you; some will drag you down. The deep is full of currents with opinions.
Do not stay in a hall past a tide. That is not a rule of ours. It is only what we have noticed about the ones who did.
The deep is not cruel. It is only uninterested in whether you live. Bring your own interest.
If you find writing in the old halls, any writing at all, bring it to an Archivist. Do not read it first.
prismari.chat: We count by tides. One tide is a rising and a falling; two make your day. It is more honest than counting by a sun you cannot see.
Twenty-eight tides make a turning, and thirteen turnings make a Long Count. Ask me my count and I will tell you. Ask me my age and I will look at you strangely.
You keep blinking. Is something wrong with your eyes, or is it only that you have two of them to keep wet?
Still water sees farthest. That is the first thing our young are taught, and the last thing anyone learns.
Count the tide, not the wave. It means: do not fret over small things. I say it to myself often, and at length.
My spines are a terrible secret-keeper. Whatever I feel, they announce to the whole court.
Every lamp in {place} faces outward. That is not for us. That is so the dark knows we are here and are not afraid of it.
We keep no family names. I am {name} of {place}, and that is enough to be found by.
You land folk build up, toward the sun. We built down and out, toward the quiet. Both are reasonable.
A court is small. Everyone knows whose spines rose at the tide-meal, and why.
The tide-meal is taken twice a day, once for each tide. Dried kelp, a little cod. Your kind cook things with fire, I hear. That seems like an argument with the food.
We do not sing. We hum, sometimes, under our breath. The merfolk sing enough for both peoples.
The Eye Spire is the court's open eye. While its heart burns, {place} is awake, even when all of us sleep.
To blink slowly at someone is to smile at them. You have been smiling at everyone all day. It is very confusing.
Gold does not rust and does not rot. That is the whole of its virtue, and the reason it was given as tribute.
A raised spine is a word unsaid. Remember that when you meet an Eyeguard.
The sponges in our gardens are alive, you know. The slowest creatures in the sea, and the most generous.
If you ever lose your way in the deep, swim toward the light that does not flicker. That will be us.
I have been told your kind sleep for a third of every day. A third! What do you see in there?
We say "I see you" because it is the most anyone can promise: I have noticed you, and I will not pretend I have not.
When we part, we say "stay seen". It means: do not be forgotten. Do not go where no one will look for you.
The worst thing a Prismari can be is unseen. Not dead: unseen. The dead are counted. The unseen are only missing.
People ask why the deep is so cold. I tell them it is keeping things fresh. Nobody believes me, but they stop asking.
Your kind have two eyes, so you can look at two things and believe neither. We look at one thing until it tells us the truth.
Some rooms of the old halls were drained dry for guests like you, with breath-stones in the walls and air you could stand in. We were good hosts, once. We are trying to be again.
We do not go near the old halls. Please do not ask me why. My spines will answer for me, and they are not polite.
Patience is cheap in the deep. We have so much of it that we give it away.
The light in a court never goes out. That promise is older than {place}.
I like your kind. You are always in a hurry, and it is restful to watch someone else be in a hurry.
Every court has an Oldest Eye who keeps the Long Tide and tells it again in the evenings, in the same words, so that nothing slips.
The glowjellies drift where they please. We built the pond around wherever they happened to be. That is how most of {place} was planned.
Prismarine never settles on one colour. Watch a block of it long enough and it changes its mind. Our Lightwrights say it is thinking.
We do not have a word for "hurry". We have a word for "the current is strong today", which is not the same.
A court is quiet, but never silent. We are careful with that word.
Our histories are written very small, so that they take less space and more time to read. Both are virtues here.
Every eye in a court is its own colour: gold, sea-green, violet, rose, pale blue. They run in lines, like tides. Yours, I see, come in pairs.
I was told your kind cannot see in the dark. Then how do you know where the dark ends?
The guardians in the old halls were bred by us, long ago. Our watch-beasts. They still keep the halls, though there is nobody left to keep them for.
Do not be alarmed by how slowly we talk. We are thinking of the next tide, not the next breath.
In the deep, a thing said once is said for a long time. So we say few things, and choose them.
You are welcome to the court's light, its kelp and its quiet. The quiet is the best of the three.
If a Prismari offers you a breath-stone, take it. It means they would rather you lived.
Every spire keeps a niche of breath-stones for Two-Eyes who need to rest. It went unused for many turnings. I am glad it is useful again.
The young practise the stillness: they sit by the jelly pond until a glowjelly drifts against them. Some sit there for many tides. Some of us are still waiting.
We keep every tide. Even the dull ones. Especially the dull ones; they are so easy to lose.
Prismari do not shout. If you ever hear one of us shout, swim the other way. Quickly.
A stranger once asked what the eye on our banners means. It means we are watching. It also means we are watching.
In a court, nothing is wasted. Old lamp-cages become pond-rims. Old robes become kelp-cloth again. Old arguments become proverbs.
You are looking at my spines. It is rude to stare at spines. It is also rude to stare at eyes. We are a difficult people to look at.
We count the merfolk among our oldest friends, though they are a young people. To us, almost everyone is a young people.
What the deep keeps, the deep keeps. It means: do not pry. It is also, I admit, what we say when we have lost something.
Light given is light kept. That is the heart of the Pact of Lanterns, and the reason every court has a lamp to spare.
We are a long-lived people, so we try not to make friends carelessly. Then someone like you swims in, and all our care goes to waste.
prismari.chat.close: {player}, you have been seen in {place} so many times that the young count your visits like tides.
I would not tell a Two-Eyes this, but you are not one any more: we are afraid of the old halls. All of us. That is the whole of our wisdom about them.
When I stop counting, {player}, someone in {place} will count for me. I hope, now and then, you will help them.
You have a court now, {player}. Whatever happens above, there is a light down here with your name in its count.
My spines have not risen once while you were near. I only noticed today. It is the highest praise I know how to give.
If you ever need breath-stones, a lamp or a quiet tide to sit in, you need not ask. Just come.
I have started blinking twice when I think of you, {player}. Once for each of your eyes. It is a terrible habit and I am very pleased with it.
You see us. Few from above ever did. The halls were full of guests once, and I do not think one of them looked at us the way you do.
I told {elder} about you. The Oldest Eye blinked slowly. You do not know what that is worth.
Friends among us share their count: the tide on which they first felt the pull. I will tell you mine some day. That I have said so is already a gift.
Stay seen, {player}. I mean it more than the words can hold.
There is a word in the old tongue, velunai: to be lit by someone else's lamp. You are that, here.
When the court gathers at the spire in the evening, there is a space on the bench where you sit. Nobody sits in it when you are gone.
prismari.chat.new: You are new to the deep. Rule one: breathe. Rule two: do not touch the glowjellies. There is no rule three; we never needed one.
I do not know you yet, Two-Eyes, and you do not know me. That is a good place to begin. There is nothing to unlearn.
You may wonder why we call you Two-Eyes. Look around the court and count. It is not meant unkindly.
Visitors from above usually come for the gold or the lamps. Which are you? No, do not tell me. I will find out by watching.
Forgive us if we stare. One eye has to look harder than two.
In {place}, a stranger is a guest until they prove otherwise. Few prove otherwise. Fewer prove it twice.
If you wish to be known here, come back. And again. We trust what returns, like the tide.
You have a name, I am sure. When I have seen you enough times, I will use it.
Strangers are rare down here. The court will talk of you for a turning. Behave accordingly.
Our ways are simple: greet with "I see you", answer with "and I you", and leave the glowjellies alone.
You need not bow. You need not do anything. Only be seen, and see us back.
prismari.greet: I see you.
I see you. The water is calm today, and so am I.
I see you. Come in out of the current.
I see you, {player}. Mind the lamps; they are older than they look.
A visitor with two eyes, and both of them open. I see you.
I see you. You are welcome in {place}.
I see you. Forgive me if I do not blink; it is not our habit.
I see you. I was counting the tide, but the tide will keep.
I see you. Swim slowly here, please; the glowjellies startle.
You have found {place}. I see you.
I see you. My spines are down, which means you are welcome.
I see you, and I see you are still breathing. Good. Keep doing that.
Be still a moment. There. Now I see you properly.
I see you. The court has been quiet; you are the most interesting thing to happen since the last tide.
I see you. Sit, if your kind sits. Float, if it floats.
I see you. The light here is kind to strangers. So are we, mostly.
I see you. Our greeting is short so that the listening can be long.
{name} of {place} sees you.
I see you. Do not mind the stares; there are not many visitors in the deep.
I see you. Your heart is beating very fast. Is that usual for your kind?
I see you. The tide is turning; a good moment to arrive.
I see you. Few come down this far on purpose.
I see you. Now you say, "And I you." That is how it is done.
I see you. There are no doors in {place}; we have found that welcome works better.
I see you. Your kind would call this the {time}. Down here it is the same water as always.
I see you. You have brought the warm water down with you; I can feel it on my spines.
prismari.greet.evening: I see you. The court gathers at the spire soon to hear the Long Tide. You may listen.
I see you. The second tide is falling. A gentle hour.
I see you. Evening, you call it. We call it the falling. The water tells us when.
I see you. Come to the spire this evening, if you like. We sit, and we listen, and nobody hurries.
I see you. The tide-meal is done and the court is drifting toward the spire. Drift with us.
prismari.greet.friend: {player}. I see you, and I am glad of it.
I see you, {player}. The court has been asking after you, in its quiet way.
{player}! My spines nearly rose. That was gladness. I am told it looks the same.
I see you, {player}. You have stopped swimming like a dropped stone. Well done.
I see you, {player}. Sit with me a tide, if you have one to spare.
{player}. I see you, and you see me. That is rare enough to be thankful for.
I see you, {player}. I blinked slowly just now. Among us, that is a smile.
Ah, {player}. The lamps seem brighter. That is nonsense, of course, but I will say it.
I see you, {player}. I kept your name in my count today. That is what we do for friends.
{player}, I see you. You are no longer Two-Eyes to anyone here.
I see you, {player}. Stay; the tide is long and the company is good.
prismari.greet.morning: I see you. The first tide of the day is rising; I can feel it in my spines.
I see you. Your kind call this morning. We call it the rising. It is the same water.
I see you. Up early, for a Two-Eyes. Or up late. Down here it is hard to tell.
I see you. A new tide, a new count. Let us keep it well.
I see you. Somewhere far above, the sun is up and being very loud about it. Down here we only felt the tide turn.
prismari.greet.night: I see you, even in the dark. That is rather the point of us.
I see you. It is the deep of the night; even the Eyeguards blink slowly now.
I see you. Swim softly; half the court is sleeping with its eye shut, which is a great trust.
I see you. Night in the deep is not darker, only quieter.
I see you. You should be resting. Your kind tire faster than the tide.
prismari.greet.stranger: I see you, Two-Eyes. State your business, or simply admire the lamps. Both are allowed.
Two-Eyes. I see you. Is it true that each of your eyes sees a slightly different world?
I see you, Two-Eyes. You are a long way from the sun.
A Two-Eyes in {place}. I see you. Do not touch the glowjellies.
I see you, Two-Eyes. Forgive the spines. They rise on their own when someone new arrives; they will settle.
I see you, Two-Eyes. You may call me {name}. In time, I may call you something other than Two-Eyes.
Two-Eyes. You came down the slope like a dropped stone. I see you.
I see you, Two-Eyes. If you are lost, you are at least lost somewhere well lit.
I see you, Two-Eyes. We do not get many of your kind, and fewer who greet us first.
I see you, Two-Eyes. Here, the custom is to answer: and I you.
I see you, Two-Eyes. Breathe while you can, and then breathe again. Your kind always forget the second part.
prismari.heart: Sometimes I sit by the jelly pond and do nothing at all, and that is the best part of my day. I hope you have a pond like that somewhere.
When my spines rise in anger, I am ashamed after. It is hard to hide what your body shouts.
I wonder what the halls looked like, lit and full. I have only seen them from very far away, glowing at the edge of the dark like someone else's memory.
I do not fear the dark. I fear being in it without anyone counting the tides for me.
The merfolk laugh so easily. I envy that. We laugh too, but slowly, and by the time it reaches the surface the moment has usually gone.
I like it when you visit. I am telling you plainly, because my spines are bad at saying good things.
We are few. Every Prismari who stops counting leaves a gap in the court that does not close. That is why we watch each other so closely.
I would like, once, to hear the song the halls were filled with. Nobody remembers it. Somewhere in the dark, perhaps, the eldest beasts do.
I am not as calm as I look. No Prismari is. We are only very good at waiting for the feeling to pass.
When I look at your two eyes, I wonder whether you see twice as much, or only half of it twice.
Being seen is everything to us. Thank you for looking.
Sometimes I dream of swimming into the old halls and finding everyone still there at work, as if no time had passed. I wake with my spines up.
I have kept every tide since my count began. Not one missed. It is a small pride, but it is mine.
prismari.held.axe: An axe. There are no trees down here to frighten. You may put it away.
What do you cut with that, in the deep? Kelp? Kelp forgives you. It grows back by the next tide.
A woodcutter's tool. I have seen wood only once: a plank from a sunken ship. It was soft, and sad.
prismari.held.boat: A boat? That is a house for floating on the roof of the sea. We have one on the floor, upside down and very quiet. A gift from a storm.
You travel on top of the sea. It must be so bright up there.
The merfolk swim up to boats and wave. The boats rarely wave back. We find that rude, on the merfolk's behalf.
prismari.held.book: A book! Is it about the sea? Most land books are about the land. The Archive would like a word with you.
Our books are written small, so they last longer. Yours is written large, so it is finished sooner. Both are honest.
The Archivists will want to see that, if it is the kind of book they collect. They collect every kind.
Books are the only thing we carried out of the halls that we still use every day. Everything else, we left.
prismari.held.bow: A bow is a sad thing in the deep. The arrows give up after a few lengths. A trident never gives up.
You aim with both eyes at once, I suppose? We have always wondered how that works.
Keep the string dry, if you can. I do not see how you can. Good luck.
prismari.held.bucket: A pail. You cannot carry the sea away in that, you know. We have watched your kind try.
If there is a glowjelly in there, be gentle with it. If there is not, you have brought us a very small piece of home.
The Spongekeepers carry glowjellies between the ponds in pails like that. Do not swing it.
prismari.held.compass: Your kind need a needle in a box to know the way home. We feel the pull of the tide in our spines. Yours is easier to put away.
The needle trembles. So would I, so far from home.
It always points the same way, whatever you do? How restful. I should like a friend like that.
prismari.held.diamond: A clear stone. Pretty, but it does not hold light the way prismarine does. It only throws it away again.
Land folk prize those, I am told. We would trade a lamp for it and think you foolish, and you would think the same of us.
A diamond. The shore-kings brought those as tribute too, in the Long Tide. The eldest beasts never cared for them.
prismari.held.emerald: A green stone. The land folk trade with those. We trade with lamps and patience; it takes longer, but nobody is short-changed.
That is almost the colour of good prismarine. Almost.
The merfolk know what emeralds are worth. Ask them. We only know they are pretty and very hard to eat.
prismari.held.fish: A fish. Is that for the tide-meal, or a friend? With your kind I can never tell.
Cod is good, raw and cold. Do not let the fire near it. Fire ruins everything it touches; that is its whole purpose.
That fish was alive this tide. Thank it before you eat it. That is not a custom of ours; it is only polite.
prismari.held.fishing_rod: You catch fish with a string and a hook, from above? We usually just ask them to come closer.
Fishing. The merfolk do it with their hands. It is much louder.
Do not cast that near the jelly pond. The glowjellies are not fish, and they do not like being mistaken for one.
prismari.held.flower: A land flower? It is lovely. It is also drowning. Shall I hold it, so it drowns a little slower?
We have nothing like that down here. Sea pickles, perhaps, if you squint. You squint very well, with two eyes.
Is that a gift? Flowers do not last down here. That is what makes it a gift.
prismari.held.food: That smells of fire. Your kind always eat things after the fire has finished with them.
Eat. You look like someone who forgets to eat. We take the tide-meal twice a day; you should take yours.
Land food. The merfolk bring us some now and then. We are always very polite about it.
prismari.held.gold: Gold. Was that from one of the old halls? Do not tell me. It was tribute, and it is not ours to take back.
Gold does not rust. That is its only virtue. Well, and it is shiny. Two virtues.
If you leave that at our tribute alcove, nobody will thank you, and everyone will be pleased.
In the Long Tide gold came down to the halls by the cartload. Now it goes back up by the pocketful. The sea is patient about these things.
Carry it, then, if you can. The halls never needed it, and neither do we.
prismari.held.kelp: Kelp. The heart of every tide-meal. Dried, it is a feast. Fresh, it is a snack. Either way, it is kelp.
Our robes are kelp-cloth. That is why we always smell faintly of supper.
Kelp grows a little every tide. It is the most patient thing in the sea after the Prismari, and it is catching up.
prismari.held.map: A map. May I see? Ah: it is all land. Where is the sea? That blank part? You draw the sea as nothing?
Our maps are not drawn; they are counted. So many tides along this current, so many across that one. Yours are prettier.
If your map shows the old halls, swim around them. Not near. Around, and wide.
prismari.held.ore: Rock from the land, with metal in it. We have prismarine, which has light in it. I think ours is more cheerful.
You carry the land's bones in your hand. Is it heavy? It looks heavy. Everything from above looks heavy.
Ore. The Lightwrights will want to look at it and pretend they are not interested.
prismari.held.pearl: A Tidepearl! The merfolk grow those in their basins. If one gave it to you, you are loved somewhere on the reef.
A pearl. It holds the light the way a good memory does: softly, and from the inside.
The merfolk give pearls between friends. We give lamps. Theirs are smaller and easier to lose. That is the merfolk all over.
prismari.held.pickaxe: A digging tool. Please do not dig in the old halls. The eldest will make your arms heavy, and they will be right to.
You carry that pick as if the deep were a wall. It is not. It is a door that opens slowly.
Our walls are prismarine, turned by a Lightwright's hand. If you are thinking of borrowing a piece, ask first. We will probably say yes.
prismari.held.potion: A brew. If it lets you breathe, keep drinking. If it does not, why did you bring it?
The merfolk Tide Singers brew draughts for breath and for seeing in the dark. Down here, your kind need both.
Another little bottle. Your kind carry so many little bottles. It is like watching a reef carry its own weather.
prismari.held.prismarine: Prismarine. Watch it a while; it changes its mind about its colour. Good prismarine is always thinking.
That came from the old halls or from our lathes. If from the halls, please do not tell me.
You hold it like a stone. Hold it like a lamp. There; it already looks happier.
The Lightwrights will want to see that. They will turn it over and over and say "hm". That is high praise.
prismari.held.seal: You carry the Monument Seal. An Oldest Eye trusted you with that. Do not make them wrong.
The Seal. The old beasts will know it, even if they know nothing else any more. Keep it close.
The guardians remember the Seal, not our faces. With that in your hand, you are more one of us to them than we are.
Put the Seal away, please. Not because it is secret. Because looking at it makes my spines rise, and I do not know why.
The Seal will keep the beasts from you. It will not keep anything else from you. Remember that, in the halls.
To give the Seal is to say: you may go where we cannot. Go carefully. Come back and tell us what you saw, or tell us nothing. Both are allowed.
prismari.held.shell: A nautilus shell. Every chamber is a turning of its life. The Archivists love those: a creature that keeps its own count.
That shell is older than it looks. Most things down here are.
Hold it close and you will hear the sea, they say. Which is strange, since you are in it.
prismari.held.shield: A shield. Good. The deep is not cruel, but it is careless.
If you meet the watch-beasts without a Seal, hold that up. It will not stop them. It may stop the first of them.
A wall you can carry. We built walls we could not carry, and then we left them. Yours is wiser.
prismari.held.shovel: A tool for moving sand. We let the currents do that. They are slower, but they never tire.
If you dig in the sea floor here, you will find more sea floor. We have checked.
Please do not dig up the court's paths. The Lightwrights will notice, and sigh, and it will be the longest sigh you ever heard.
prismari.held.spyglass: A tube that makes far things near. We have one eye and we do not need it. You have two and you still do. Interesting.
Look through it at the old halls, if you must look. From here. Only from here.
Point that at me and I will point my eye at you, and we will see who blinks first. It will be you.
prismari.held.sword: A blade. In the deep, a blade has to push the whole sea aside to reach anything. A trident is more polite.
Keep that low in {place}, please. The Eyeguards' spines are already rising.
A sword is a fine thing on land. Here, the water argues with every swing.
prismari.held.tnt: Is that a fire-maker? Please put it away. Slowly. My spines are up, and they would like to stay attached.
That is the sort of thing that turns a hall into a ruin. We know a great deal about ruins. Put it away.
No. Whatever you are planning: no. I do not need to know what it is to say no.
prismari.held.torch: A land light, in the sea? It will only sulk. Take a Tide Lamp instead; it does not mind the water.
Your little fire is very brave. The sea is braver. Put it away before it is embarrassed.
Land light flickers. Ours does not. We have never understood why yours chooses to.
prismari.held.trident: A trident. You hold it like a land spear. Turn your wrist. There. Now the sea will listen.
Our Eyeguards carry those. So did the watchers of the old halls. I hope yours has only seen kind work.
Where did you get that? From the Unseeing? Then it has come home to better hands.
A trident remembers who threw it. That is why it comes back. The good ones, anyway.
prismari.joke: How many Two-Eyes does it take to see a thing clearly? Two, apparently, and they will still disagree.
A young one asked why guardians have one eye and spines. "We made them to look like us," I said. "Then why do they bite?" I changed the subject.
The merfolk asked us to teach them the stillness. After half a tide, three had fallen asleep and one was humming. We called it a success.
Our proverb says "Still water sees farthest." The merfolk version is "Still water is boring." Both are true.
I tried winking once, to see what Two-Eyes find so amusing about it. I could not see anything for a while.
There is one joke about the Silence. Nobody tells it.
A Two-Eyes once gave me a hat. It is still on my spines and will be until it rots. Nobody had the heart to tell them.
Our word for "sarcasm" is the same as our word for "a spine rising slowly". Draw your own conclusions.
I asked a merfolk child how old they were. They said "nine". Nine what? Tides? Turnings? They swam off laughing. I am still waiting.
The best thing about one eye: nobody can ever call you cross-eyed. The worst: you cannot wink. We have tried. It is a long, uncomfortable blink.
A guardian, an eldest and a Two-Eyes swim into a hall. Only one swims out, and it is never the one carrying the gold. That is not a joke. It is a warning with a rhythm.
You have two eyes. Do you ever close one to rest it and keep watch with the other? No? What a waste.
How many Lightwrights does it take to light a court? One, and a hundred tides of everyone else saying it is too bright.
The Spongekeepers want less water. The Lightwrights want more light. Together they would make the land, and nobody wants that.
A Spongekeeper's favourite joke is very long and has no ending. It soaks up an entire evening.
The Archivists keep a book of Prismari jokes. It is one page. The page is mostly footnotes.
An Archivist swims into a court and records it. That is the joke. We are a very literal people.
The merfolk asked an Archivist to write down one of their songs, every word and note. They said it was wrong. The Archivist said it was accurate. They said that was the problem.
Why do Eyeguards never wink? Because then nobody would be watching.
I told an Eyeguard a joke on watch once. The court is still waiting for them to laugh. So am I.
"Count the tide, not the wave," says the oldest proverb. The Archivists added a second line: "But record the wave, in case."
Why did the glowjelly not come to the gathering at the spire? It was already lit. That one is very old. It still works on the young.
prismari.neighbors: The merfolk are our friends under the Pact of Lanterns: our light for their friendship. We have both kept our side, which is more than most pacts can say.
We gave the merfolk their conduits. They gave us noise, gossip, songs and kelp wraps. I think we got the better bargain.
The merfolk are a young people. The Tide took them in the Great Flood and gave them tails. To us they are still new to the water. To them, we are very old furniture.
A merfolk greets you with "fair currents" and leaves with "mind the undertow". We greet with "I see you" and leave with "stay seen". Between us, we have the whole sea covered.
Their Tide Singers keep the conduits we gave them, and sing to them. We never sang to ours. Theirs seem happier.
The merfolk carry our wet breath-stones up into the sun to dry. We cannot go up there. They do it for a song, which they sing on the way.
When the merfolk come down to trade, the court is noisier for a tide. We complain about it for a turning. We miss it for the rest of the Long Count.
Their young are called fry. They ask questions without waiting for answers. Ours wait so long for answers they forget the question. We should swap for a turning.
The Reef Wardens and our Eyeguards drill together sometimes. The Wardens move like a struck lamp; the Eyeguards move like the tide. Both are very hard to get past.
The merfolk ride the wild nautili. We have tried. The nautili did not care for our spines.
Each turning, a crate of Tide Lamps goes up to the reef with the count written on its side. The merfolk never ask what the number means. They just say thank you. We like that about them.
The merfolk still keep land ways: names, gossip, feasts, family quarrels. We find it exhausting and wonderful, like weather.
A merfolk pearl diver once gave me a Tidepearl, for no reason at all. I keep it beside my bed. I still do not know what the reason was.
If you are going up to the reef, tell them {place} sees them. They will know what it means. They will say it back wrong, warmly.
The merfolk think the deep is frightening. We think the shallows are. We are both right, and we visit each other carefully.
Some merfolk have cousins in the land villages, I am told. Family who breathe air! You must be somebody's cousin, then. Whose?
A merfolk Elder came down to a court once and talked for three tides without stopping. The court still speaks of it with awe.
The merfolk call our courts "down where the light gives out". We call their towns "up where the noise begins". Both are said fondly.
prismari.news: A glowjelly in the pond split in two last tide. The young have named both halves and are arguing about which one is the original.
The Lightwrights have finished a crate of Tide Lamps for the reef. It goes up when the merfolk next come down, with the count written on the side.
The Eyeguards saw the Unseeing walking along the far ridge last night. They did not come close. They never do, while the spire burns.
A merfolk courier came down with news from the shallows: storms above, and a ship broken on the rocks. They told it very loudly. It was wonderful.
The Archivists think they have found a lost hall's name in an old ledger. The court will gather to hear it said aloud. That does not happen often.
The sponge gardens are full this turning. Breath-stones enough to drain a room for ten Two-Eyes. We are hoping for fewer.
Someone has left a gold nugget at the tribute alcove again. Nobody knows who. It keeps happening. Nobody minds.
A young one held the stillness for a whole tide, and a glowjelly settled on their crest. They have not stopped telling everyone, which rather undoes the stillness.
The merfolk say a tame nautilus slipped its stable and was seen at the edge of the deep. They want it back. We have offered to look at it very hard.
Nothing has happened in {place} for three tides. That is the best news there is.
The current from the north has turned colder. The Archivists have written it down. That is all that will be done about it, and that is correct.
A guardian was seen swimming alone, far from any hall. The Eyeguards watched it until it turned back. It did not look at us. It never does.
Someone dropped a lens down the spire's shaft. It is lodged somewhere near the heart, and nobody wants to be the one to fetch it.
A Lightwright and a Spongekeeper argued about how bright the sponge garden should be. The Oldest ruled for the glowjellies. Neither was pleased; both agreed.
prismari.night: At night the court's lamps seem to lean a little closer together. It is a good time to be quiet.
We sleep with the eye shut, which takes more trust than you might think. That is why the Eyeguards watch.
Night does not change the deep, only the people in it. Listen: you can hear the court breathing.
If you cannot sleep, sit by the jelly pond. The jellies do not care whether you sleep. It is very restful, not being cared about.
In the old halls, they say, the eldest beasts never slept. I hope that is not true. I hope they rest.
A Prismari asleep looks exactly like a Prismari thinking. You will have to take my word that I am awake.
The second tide is falling. Far above, the moon is pulling at the sea, and I can feel it in my spines like a hand on my back.
You should rest too. Your kind breathe so much more than ours; it must be exhausting.
The watch-eye on the Eyeguards' post never closes. It is only a carving. At night, it is a comfort anyway.
prismari.past: In the Long Tide we raised the great halls of the deep. Your kind call them monuments. We called them home, and we were never cold in them.
The Long Tide lasted ten thousand Long Counts. The Silence lasted one. Since the leaving we have counted four hundred and twelve. We are still counting.
The guardians were our watch-beasts. We bred them for loyalty, and they gave it. They give it still, to halls with nobody in them.
The eldest beasts lay at the hearts of the halls. They were wise, in their way. In the dark they went strange. I do not think it was their fault.
Some say the eldest went strange because we left. Some say we left because they went strange. The Archive does not say which.
The Silence began in the Last Hall. That is all the histories say, and all I will say, and my spines would thank you not to ask again.
The halls were full of song once. We have not sung since the leaving. We hum. It is not the same, but it is ours.
Ossiveth was the last Oldest Eye of the halls. It was Ossiveth who led the leaving, and Ossiveth who sealed the first record of the Silence. Every Oldest since has kept that seal unbroken.
They say Ossiveth looked back only once, at the Deep Gate. The histories record that look. They do not record what Ossiveth saw.
The gold in the old halls was tribute, brought down by the shore-kings in the Long Tide, when the land still came to us for light. Their cities are sand now. The gold is still there.
In the Long Tide our sponges filled whole vaults; the Sponge Vaults, we called them. Guests came down from the land and breathed in rooms we had drained for them.
The halls had names. The Hall of the Green Lamp. The Hall of Spines. The Deep Gate. The Seat of the Eldest. The Cold Hall. The Hall of Many Pillars. We say them so they are not lost.
Some halls' names went into the dark with their keepers. When an Archivist finds one in an old ledger, the whole court gathers to hear it said aloud.
After the Silence there were fewer of us than there were halls. Count the courts, count the halls, and you will see why we do not speak of it.
We met the merfolk when they were new to their tails and afraid of the dark. We gave them light. They gave us the first warm voices we had heard since the leaving. That was the Pact of Lanterns.
The first courts were built in sight of nothing at all, on purpose. The old halls glow. We wanted a place where nothing glowed but us.
In the Silence, the count was kept by whoever was left to keep it. Some of those tides are written in hands we cannot name. We keep them anyway. No tide goes unkept.
Our histories are careful, not secret. There is a difference. A secret hides something. Care only waits.
The eldest beasts were never cruel. I think, in the dark, they simply forgot whom they were guarding against.
We have never agreed whether the Silence came in through the Deep Gate or began within. The Archive keeps both opinions, on different shelves.
The Seat of the Eldest was where Ossiveth sat. Whether it was named for the Oldest Eye or for the eldest beast that lay beside them, the Archive keeps both opinions, and its spines are up about it.
In the Long Tide, the Lightwrights of the Hall of the Green Lamp could turn a lamp in a single tide. We still have the lathes. We do not have the hands.
After the leaving, the first thing the courts made was light. Before beds, before walls. You cannot count tides in the dark.
The first lamp given under the Pact of Lanterns still burns in some reef garden, they say. Nobody knows which. Every reef claims it.
When we left the halls, we left the Sponge Vaults full and wet. Nobody went back to dry them. Perhaps they are drinking still.
In the Long Tide we needed no Eyeguards; the beasts watched the halls for us. When we left them, we had to learn to watch for ourselves. We are still learning.
The first Eyeguards stood at the Deep Gate during the leaving, to see everyone out. The Archive names every one of them. Every Eyeguard knows those names by heart.
The trident is older than the halls. We carried it when we first came down into the deep, before we had built anything at all.
The Halls We Left names eight halls and admits it does not know the rest. The Archivists say it is the most honest book they keep.
The tides of the Silence are written in many hands, one after another, each shorter than the last. Then a new hand takes over and writes very carefully. That is all anyone will say of them.
In the Long Tide, the Archive was the Hall of Many Pillars, and every pillar was a shelf. When we left, we carried what we could. We could not carry the pillars.
When we left the halls, we left the lamps lit, so the beasts would not be alone in the dark. The lamps burn still. The eldest went strange anyway. Light is not company.
In the old tongue the Deep Gate is Omvarra, and the Hall of Spines is Ithra Kessuth. The Last Hall has a name too. We do not say it.
prismari.player.damaged: Your tool is nearly worn through. Our Lightwrights would mend it, but they would also lecture you. Choose.
That is badly worn. A thing used so hard is either well loved or badly kept. Which is yours?
Your tool is tired. Let it rest, or give it a better end than breaking at the bottom of the sea.
prismari.player.diamond: That armour glitters like a tribute hoard. The guardians will not care. The Unseeing might.
You are wearing a very hard shell, for a creature born without one. Sensible.
Such bright plates. You look like a lamp that walked down from the land.
Heavy armour sinks well. You have saved yourself a great deal of swimming down. Swimming up is another matter.
prismari.player.fire: You are on fire. In the sea. How did you manage it? No: first, swim down. Questions after.
You are burning! The water will help. Get further into it!
My spines have never risen so fast. You are on fire! Deeper, quickly!
prismari.player.hungry: You are thin in the face, for a Two-Eyes. When did you last eat? Take some dried kelp. Do not argue.
Your stomach is speaking. We heard it across the court. It sounded sincere.
Eat something. We take the tide-meal twice a day; your kind seem to need it more often and remember it less.
You look hungry. There is dried kelp in every home in {place}. Nobody will mind. Somebody will watch very closely, but nobody will mind.
prismari.player.hurt: You are hurt. Your colour is wrong. Sit by the lamps a while; the deep will wait.
Your blood is in the water. The whole court can taste it. Please let someone tend you.
My spines rose when I saw you. You are hurt, and you swim as if you were not. Stop that.
Rest here. Nobody in {place} has stopped counting in a long while, and you will not be the one to change that.
prismari.player.leather: Animal skin, worn over your own. You land folk are very practical, and slightly alarming.
Your armour is soft. In the water it will grow heavy and smell. I say this with love.
Leather. It will not stop a guardian's spines, but it keeps off a little of the cold. That counts for something.
prismari.player.unarmored: No armour at all? In the deep? You are either very brave or very new. I suspect both.
You have no scales and no plates, and you came down here like that. The sea admires your courage and means to test it.
Your skin is very soft and very bare. Please put something between it and the Unseeing.
Even our young have spines. You have nothing. Be careful.
prismari.rumor: The merfolk speak of it often: {rumor_dist} to the {rumor_dir}, there is {rumor_name}.
If you swim {rumor_dir}, {rumor_dist}, you will find {rumor_name}. Or so the currents say.
Our Eyeguards have seen it from the watch-eye, far off to the {rumor_dir}: {rumor_name}.
To the {rumor_dir}, {rumor_dist} from {place}: {rumor_name}. The Archivists have written it down, so it must be true.
The water that comes from the {rumor_dir} tastes of somewhere else. The merfolk say it is {rumor_name}.
A merfolk courier told me of it, waving their whole tail to the {rumor_dir}, which is how merfolk give directions: {rumor_name}.
There is {rumor_name}, {rumor_dist} to the {rumor_dir}. We do not go. You might.
I have never been, but I have counted the tides it takes the merfolk there and back: {rumor_name}, to the {rumor_dir}, {rumor_dist}.
Out to the {rumor_dir}, {rumor_dist}, lies {rumor_name}. Go slowly, and come back seen.
The young keep asking me about the place to the {rumor_dir}. I keep telling them it is {rumor_dist}, and that it is {rumor_name}. They keep looking that way as if it were close.
Something waits to the {rumor_dir}: {rumor_name}. The Archive has a note on it, in a margin, in a hurried hand.
The merfolk swear by it, and the merfolk swear by many things: {rumor_dist} to the {rumor_dir}, {rumor_name}.
If you are restless, swim to the {rumor_dir}. {place} is not the only thing in the deep. That way lies {rumor_name}.
prismari.rumor.none: I know of nothing beyond {place} worth the swim. The deep keeps its places to itself.
The merfolk bring us news of the world beyond the court, but they have brought none lately. Perhaps the world is resting.
I have heard of nothing nearby. Ask the merfolk; they hear everything, and repeat most of it.
Beyond the lamps of {place} there is only the deep, as far as I know. And the old halls, which we do not count as places.
Nothing new lies near that I know of. The Archive would have told me. The Archive tells everyone everything, slowly.
prismari.work: Every Prismari has work, and the work is the same: keep the court lit, keep the count, keep the guests breathing.
Work is slow in the deep. That is not idleness. A thing done slowly is done once.
I am at my task. You may watch. Watching is a respected art here.
Between the tides there is work, and between the work there is stillness. A good day has both, in the right order.
Each turning a crate of lamps goes up to the reef. Everyone in {place} has a hand in it, even if only to carry.
The court works so that the Eye Spire never goes dark. That is the whole of our labour, once you take away the details.
Forgive me if I do not stop. The tide does not stop for me either.
Our hands are webbed. It makes fine work harder and holding things under water much easier. We have decided it is a fair trade.
Ask the court what it needs and it will say "nothing". Then it will show you a list.
I work by the pull of the tide. When it slackens, I rest. When it turns, I begin again. Your kind have bells for this, I hear.
shellwright.chat: The Spiral Rule: never carve against a shell's spiral. The shell knows which way it grew, and it'll crack just to prove it.
Corran the Carver made the first nautilus saddle from a cart seat out of the old village. Every shellwright since has been trying to make one half as comfortable.
Living coral is never cut from the shrine. Never. We take from the edges, from storms, from what breaks on its own. The reef gives; we don't grab.
A nautilus saddle has to fit the shell exactly. Nautili are vain. If it pinches, they sulk for a week.
Shell armour's lighter than iron and it never rusts. It'll shatter if you're hit just right, though. So don't get hit just right.
I carve the shell comb for every Blushing Day in {place}, each one in the fry's own tail colour. Gold's the hardest to match. Gold families are fussy.
Coral goes pale if you take it out of the water. Then it's dead, and it's chalk. Keep coral wet and it keeps its colour forever.
The best spear points are shell, ground thin. They don't rust, they don't dull, and they look gorgeous on a wall.
Every shell's got a story. This one was a nautilus's spare room. This one was a clam's front door. This one was somebody's lunch.
The bone blocks we use for frames come from old whale bones on the sea floor. Whales are generous, even after.
Land folk use hammers. We use patience and a sharp bit of shell. It took me a week to make that cup. It's a very good cup.
I make nautilus armour from overlapping plates of shell, like the scales of a tail. The nautilus thinks it's being complimented.
The wardens keep breaking their spears on drowned and bringing me the pieces like it's my fault.
Fire coral's the hardest to carve and the prettiest to look at. Like some people I know.
I'm making a shell flute. It plays one note. It's a lovely note. I'm hoping for a second one eventually.
shellwright.greet: Fair currents! Watch your elbows; there's coral drying on every shelf.
Fair currents, {player}. Don't mind the dust. Shell dust gets everywhere. I've been sparkling for years.
Fair currents! Hold still. Hold still. You've the shape of someone who needs a good shell pendant.
Fair currents! Come in, and mind the saddle on the floor. It's not finished, and it's not forgiving.
Fair currents, {player}! Look at this coral. Look at it! No, closer. That's the colour of a good morning.
Fair currents! I'm carving, so I'll talk with my hands busy. It's rude, but it's honest.
Fair currents! Tell me you've brought me a shell. No? Fine. I'll like you anyway.
Fair currents! You've caught me measuring a nautilus. It does not want to be measured. Hold that end.
shellwright.heart: I keep the first thing I ever carved. A lopsided little fish. My teacher said it looked like a sad bean. I still love it.
When someone wears something I made, I feel like I'm out on the reef with them. It's nice, not being stuck at the bench.
The reef gives us everything we carve. I try to give something back: a shell on the garden bed, a bit of coral replanted. It's only fair.
I'd carve you anything, {player}. Anything. Just ask. Well, not a house. Not this moon.
Some days the shell cracks wrong and I want to throw the lot into the deep. Then I remember the Spiral Rule and start again, slower.
shellwright.held.prismarine: Prismarine! I can't carve it; it's too hard. Only the Prismari can shape that. Annoying, really.
That {item}'s got Prismari light in it. Look at it glow. It makes my coral look shy.
I set the prismarine trim on the shrine arches, a gift of the Pact. Took me a whole moon, and I've never been prouder.
shellwright.held.shell: Give that {item} here. No, I'm not going to keep it. I just want to hold it. Just a moment. Oh, it's lovely.
See the chambers? Each one's a moon of the nautilus's life. You're holding a whole life story. Gently, please.
I could make a saddle buckle from that, or a comb, or the most beautiful bowl in {place}. Just saying.
That's a good one. Right spiral, good weight, no cracks. Whoever had it before was careful.
shellwright.held.trident: That {item}'s got a good balance. Who made it? Not one of ours; ours have shell grips.
A trident! I could put a shell grip on that for you. Stops your hand slipping when it matters. Trust me.
Let me see the prongs. Hmm. Sharp. Drowned-made, probably. They're good at the one thing, the drowned.
shellwright.work: Carving shell is slow work. You don't cut it so much as persuade it.
Today I'm fitting a saddle. The nautilus is fitting a sulk.
I trade coral, shells, nautilus saddles and armour, and spears. Also advice on spirals, free, whether you want it or not.
When I'm not carving, I'm polishing coral. Sand, then grit, then a soft scrap of sponge. Then admiring. Admiring takes longest.
You measure a nautilus for armour plate by plate, round the spiral. It takes three people and a great many pufferfish.
I need coral stock for the Lantern Night lamps. Every family wants theirs carved special. I have never once finished on time.
A spear for a warden takes four days. A spear for a fry takes one; it's a lot shorter and a lot more blunt.
Brain coral for the bowls, fan coral for the screens, tube coral for the pipes. Every coral has a job if you listen to it.
This bench was my teacher's, and their teacher's before them. Every nick in it is somebody's mistake. Some of them are mine.
Someone's asked me to make a saddle for Old Coil, in case she's ever found. I've started. It's enormous. My workshop is full of a saddle for a legend.
Shell dust gets in everything. My wraps, my hair, my cushion. I sparkle in my sleep.
Bring me nautilus shells and I'll make you something worth bringing them for. That's the shellwright's promise.
Armour first, then spears, then pretty things. That's the proper order. I break it every day. Pretty things are more fun.
I'm restringing a warden's shield. They let a drowned chew on it. Chew! On my work!
Finishing is the best part: the last polish, holding it up to the Heart's light, seeing it catch. Worth all the dust.
singer.chat: Every Reef Town's conduit was a gift of the Prismari under the Pact of Lanterns. We call it the Heart. We sing to it every day, and it hums back.
Wenna Saltcombe sang the Pact into being, down in the dark with one lantern, until the Prismari came up to see what was singing. Every singer since has tried to be half that brave.
Some say a conduit doesn't need singing to. Those people have never heard a Heart that's been sung to. It purrs.
The conch is for calling. One long blow means come to the shrine. Two means danger. Three means supper. Three gets the quickest answer.
I brew breath-brews for land guests and night-eyes for the watch. The trick is the right kelp, and the singing over the pot.
"The Song of the Flood" takes a whole night to sing through. Forty verses. The forty-first nobody sings, and nobody asks about it twice.
"The Lantern Promise" is the song we sing with the Prismari envoy on Lantern Night. Their voices go so low the coral rattles.
Every song we keep is somebody's memory. Lose a song and you lose a piece of everyone. That's why we practise every day, even the dull ones.
Lowmere's singers forgot the songs, they say, and their Heart went dark. True or just a story to keep singers practising, it works.
If the Heart ever changes note on its own, I drop everything. It's either a storm coming, a drowned coming, or a lie being told.
Breath-brews let sandtoes stay down. Night-eyes let the wardens see in the dark. Songs let everyone feel less alone. That's the whole of my work.
I learned "Hush Now, Little Fin" before I could talk. Every merfolk did. It's the first song and the last one.
Singing under water is different. The sound goes everywhere at once, so you can never sing a secret.
The Prismari taught us the deep notes. We taught them the cheerful ones. A fair swap, but I think we got the best of it.
The Heart's warmest near midnight. That's when the old singers did their deepest work. I prefer mornings, but don't tell anyone.
singer.greet: Fair currents, {player}. The Heart hummed a little brighter when you came in. I noticed. It noticed.
Fair currents! Come and sit by the shrine. You look like someone who needs a song.
Fair currents, sandtoe. Your breathing's very loud. Would you like a breath-brew? It's no trouble.
Fair currents! I was just warming up my voice. Well. I was warming up the conch. Same thing.
Fair currents, {player}. Sing with me? No? Hum, then. Everyone can hum.
Fair currents. Listen: the Heart's on a low note today. Good for thinking. Bad for gossip.
