Fair currents! You've the face of someone the sea's been kind to. Sit, and tell me about it.
Fair currents, friend of the dry. The Tide sees you. So do I.
singer.heart: When I sing to the Heart and it sings back, I feel like the whole sea is listening. That's a lot to feel at once. Good, though.
I'm afraid of forgetting a song. Not a verse. A whole song. Lowmere forgot, and Lowmere's gone.
I sang Wenna's verse alone once, in the dark at the shelf, just to feel what she felt. Something in the deep hummed back. I've never told anyone that.
Songs are just memories with a tune, so they don't wander off. I've got so many in me, some days I feel like a whole town.
If you ever need a song, {player}, come and ask. Even just one line. I'll find you the right one.
singer.held.potion: Let me see that brew. Hmm. Land-made. Smells of mushrooms. Ours smell of kelp and moonlight. Ours are better, but I'm biased.
Is that one of mine? It might be! I always scratch a little fin on the glass.
A brew! Drink it slowly. Brews like to be noticed.
singer.held.prismarine: Prismarine! The Prismari's stone. Hold it near the Heart and listen. Hear that? The same song in two voices.
That {item} is a piece of the deep. Every bit of prismarine in {place} came from the Prismari as a Pact gift. Keep yours kindly.
The Heart's frame is prismarine. I polish it every morning and thank the deep folk out loud. They can't hear me. I do it anyway.
singer.held.seal: The Monument Seal. Oh, {player}. The Prismari trust you. Under the Pact, that makes you nearly kin to us both.
I've only ever heard of that seal in the old songs: "the eye that sees gave a stone that is seen". I never thought I'd see one in a sandtoe's hand.
Keep that seal close. The guardians will let you pass. But keep your wits closer; the old halls are dark for a reason.
singer.work: I sing to the Heart from shimmer to dusk. Not all the time; even the Heart needs a quiet. But often.
Today I'm learning an old song. Three verses about a fish who wanted to be a bird. It's sadder than you'd think.
I brew two things, mostly: breath-brews for land guests and night-eyes for the watch. And a horrible-tasting cough brew for the fry.
Keeping the Heart is easy. Keeping it happy is the work. Song, light, company. Like anyone, really.
I make conches from the big spiral shells. Blow one and you'll swim as if the Heart's own breath were with you, for a little while.
If you want a conch, you'll need to learn to blow it. Lips like this. No, like this. Now you sound like a sad whale. Perfect.
The conch shrine keeps the old songs written in shell, a notch for every note. I read them with my fingers.
I'm practising for Lantern Night. The Prismari envoy listens very carefully. Go flat, and that great eye narrows. It's terrifying.
I trade brews and conches, and songs on request. Once a singer of this town gave a whole Heart to a reef that had lost theirs. That's the greatest gift a singer can give.
Every morning I tell the Heart the news. Who's courting, who's quarrelling, what the fry broke. It hums along. I think it likes gossip.
The hardest song is the Bell Night song. You sing every lost name. My voice goes at the same name every year, and I don't even know whose it is.
I keep the songs; the songs keep the town. That's what singers say. It sounds grand. Mostly it means a great deal of practice.
A good brew wants the right kelp, the right pickle, and the right song sung over it. Get the song wrong and it tastes of feet.
When a fry's tail blushes its colour, a singer sings the family song over them. I've done it more times than I can count. I cry at every one.
Some nights I keep the Heart company alone. It hums, I hum, the reef sleeps. It's my favourite part of the work.
spongekeeper.chat: A breath-stone is a dry sponge laid in a sealed room. It drinks the sea out of the room, and a Two-Eyes can stand there and breathe. We were famous for it, once.
A sponge is an animal. Not a plant, not a stone. An animal that has decided, very sensibly, never to move.
Wet sponges must be dried before they are breath-stones again. Nothing is dry down here, so the merfolk carry them up to the sun for us.
Glowjellies sting your kind but not ours. Nobody knows why. The jellies are not telling. I think they simply like us.
Sea pickles grow in clusters of one to four. Four is lucky. One is lonely. I move the lonely ones closer to the others.
The glowjellies are our living lamps. They need no cages and no lathes; only to be left alone and spoken to kindly. I understand them completely.
A Spongekeeper's hands are always wet. That is the joke. We are under the sea; everyone's hands are wet. We say it anyway.
In the Sponge Vaults of the Long Tide there were breath-stones enough to drain a hall. Now we have a garden. A garden is enough.
You can tell a good sponge by how slowly it drinks. The greedy ones fill too fast and tear. Patience, even in sponges.
The spire keeps a niche of breath-stones for guests who breathe air. I keep them fresh. Nobody used them for many turnings. I kept them fresh anyway.
I talk to the sponges. They do not answer. That is what makes them such good listeners.
A glowjelly has never seen the sun, and yet it knows when the tide turns. It pulses a little slower at the falling. You have to watch a long time to notice.
If a glowjelly drifts against your arm and does not sting, you are Prismari, or very lucky. Do not test which.
I carry jellies between the ponds in a pail, slowly. A jelly carried fast arrives sulking, and a sulking jelly gives no light for a tide.
Sponges grow on the racks for a turning, soak in the beds for a turning, and rest for a turning. Rest is part of the work. I am very good at that part.
Breath-stones are the oldest kindness we have. Before the halls and before the beasts, we were a people who made air for strangers.
A breath-stone that has drained a room for a guest is honoured. It sits on the top rack for a turning, where it can see the whole garden.
The garden is the quietest place in {place}. That is on purpose. Sponges hear everything and dislike most of it.
spongekeeper.greet: I see you. Step around the racks, please; the young sponges are drinking.
I see you. Do not mind the glowjellies. They are curious, not hungry. Mostly curious.
I see you. You come at a good time; the breath-stones are thirsty and I am bored.
I see you. Mind your elbows near the soaking beds. Sponges bruise, and they hold a grudge for turnings.
I see you. Welcome to the garden. Everything here is alive and very slow, including me.
I see you. There is air in your chest; I can see it. The sponges are jealous.
I see you. Pickles lit, jellies drifting, sponges drinking. All is well in the garden.
I see you. Come slowly, please. In the garden, the fastest thing is supposed to be me, and I am not fast.
spongekeeper.heart: I worry that one day no Two-Eyes will need a breath-stone again, and we will forget how to make room for strangers.
When a glowjelly drifts close and stays, I hold very still. It is the nearest thing to being chosen that I know.
I like slow things. Sponges, kelp, the tide, the court. Fast things leave before you can love them.
I have never seen the sun. The sponges have, on their trips up with the merfolk. Sometimes I hold a freshly dried one and try to imagine it.
You stood in the garden and breathed, and did not hurry. I noticed. The sponges noticed. That was the kindest thing you could have done here.
When I stop counting, I would like to be laid in the garden among the racks. The sponges will not notice. That is what I like about them.
spongekeeper.held.bucket: A pail! Are you carrying a jelly? Hold it level. No, level. There. Now it is happy.
If you bring a glowjelly home in that, speak to it kindly every tide. It will light your house and forgive you everything.
A pail is a sponge that cannot make up its mind.
spongekeeper.held.kelp: Kelp. Lay a strip over a resting sponge and it sleeps better. That is not learning; that is only kindness.
The racks are tied with kelp-cord. If that is fresh, I will trade you a pickle for it.
Fresh kelp! The young sponges like to be wrapped in it after a long soak. Do not ask me how I know. I just know.
spongekeeper.work: Tending the breath-stones. Turn them, soak them, let them rest. Sponges need rest more than anyone, except me.
These are the wet ones, waiting for the merfolk to carry them up to the sun. These are the dry ones, back from the sun. You can tell by the smell of daylight.
Wringing out sponges. It does not dry them, not down here. But it makes them feel attended to.
I am counting pickles. Four by the gate, two by the racks, one lonely one by the wall. I will move the lonely one.
The jellies need feeding. Well, they need nothing. But I like to bring them something. They ignore it. It is a good arrangement.
If you need a breath-stone, I can spare one. If you need a room drained, I will need three tides and your patience.
This rack is for the young sponges. Do not lean on it. They are impressionable.
A dry sponge lowered into the water too fast tears. Lower it slowly, like this. There. Now it is drinking.
The garden must be lit, but not too bright; sponges grow pale in strong light. The pickles are just right. The pickles always are.
I keep the glowjellies in the pond, the sponges on the racks, and the young out of both. Two out of three is a good day.
Please do not squeeze the sponges. I know. Everyone wants to. Everyone who does is sorry.
Ask the merfolk to dry your sponges and they will do it for a song. Ask them to bring them back and they will bring a song as well. They cannot help it.
I am moving a glowjelly from the garden to the pond. It took a tide to persuade it into the pail. It will take another to persuade it out. That is the job.
I check every sponge by hand, every tide. Most are fine. One or two are sulking. I sit with those a while.
warden.chat: The drowned are the ones the Tide wouldn't take. Slow, heavy, and they don't stop. We pity them. We still poke them with tridents.
"Hold the arch." That's the Warden's Oath. Stand in the archway and nothing gets past you into the town. Simple to say. Hard on a long night.
The Barnacle King? Fry story. A great drowned with a crown of barnacles, sitting on the shrine of lost Lowmere. Fry story. I keep my trident sharp anyway.
A trident's better than a sword down here. It goes through water like it was made for it. Swords drag. Swords sulk.
I ride the reef on my nautilus every afternoon: round the edges, past the gardens, along the shelf. It pretends it's a chore. It isn't; it loves it.
The first wardens fought the drowned with fence posts from the old villages. We've got tridents now. I think about those fence posts and feel very lucky.
The drowned come at night, mostly. They follow the lights. That's why the lights are inside the arches and we're outside them.
If a drowned has a trident, take it. That's the rule. Anything they'd use against us, we take back and use better.
I've polished this trident so often I can see my tail in it. Gorgeous tail. Good trident.
The guardians at the old monuments don't bother us so long as we don't bother them. That's the best kind of neighbour.
Night watch is quiet. Mostly. You get to know every shadow on the reef. Then a new shadow turns up and your scales go stiff.
We train the fry to swim fast and loud. A loud fry is a safe fry; we can always find them.
I saw Old Coil once, on night watch. White, huge, slow, out past the shelf. I didn't tell anyone for a moon. Who believes a tired warden?
Every scratch on my armour's a story. That one's a drowned. That one's a guardian. That one's a very angry clam.
The deep doesn't scare me. The shallows at night, when the lamps flicker... those scare me a bit.
warden.greet: Fair currents, {player}. Stay inside the arches and you'll be safe. That's my job: the arches.
Fair currents! Don't mind the trident. I always hold it like this. It's a comfort.
Fair currents. Seen anything shambling about past the lamps? No? Good. Tell me if you do.
Fair currents, {player}. "Hold the arch," as we say. You're on the right side of it today.
Fair currents! You've got good shoulders for a sandtoe. Ever held a trident? You should.
Fair currents. I'm on watch, but I can talk. I can always talk. Wardens are terrible gossips.
Fair currents! My nautilus likes you. It flared its tentacles. That's either fondness or hunger.
Fair currents, friend. Hold still so I can see you properly. Right. Not drowned. Welcome.
warden.heart: I don't love fighting. I love {place}. Sometimes loving it means fighting. That's the trick of it.
Every drowned I turn away was somebody once. I say "rest easy" when I send them off. They can't hear me. I say it anyway.
On long watches I think about everyone asleep behind the arches. Then the dark doesn't feel so big.
I was scared on my first night watch. I'm still scared, a bit, every time. Brave isn't not being scared. Brave is staying at the arch.
If anything ever came for you here, {player}, it would have to come through me first. I want you to know that.
warden.held.shield: Good! A shield's a warden's best friend after the trident and the nautilus. Third best friend. Still a friend.
Keep that {item} up. The drowned throw tridents, and they're not polite about where they land.
Nice shield. Mine's shell over leather. Does yours float? Mine sinks. Better for standing your ground.
warden.held.sword: A sword. It'll do in a pinch, but it's slow down here. Get a trident, friend.
That {item}'s pretty. Points beat edges under water, though. Remember that when the drowned come shambling.
I trained with a sword once, in the shallows. Felt like fighting with a kelp leaf. Never again.
warden.held.trident: That's a trident! Good. Hold it like this: thumb along the shaft. No, the other way. There. Now you look like a warden.
Took that off a drowned, did you? Well done. Every trident we take back is one less coming at us.
Let me see the balance on that {item}. Hmm. Good weight. Throw it true and it'll come home to you like a faithful nautilus.
If you ever want to train, the dummy's free. Bring that trident. It'll like the exercise.
warden.player.unarmored: No armour? Out here? I'm going to fuss. You can't stop me. Get some armour on, {player}.
You're as bare as a fry. The drowned will be delighted. I won't.
Not even a bit of shell? Right. Stay by me, and stay inside the arches until you find some.
warden.work: Drilling with the trident: thrust, twist, pull back, check the arch. A thousand times. Then a thousand more.
I keep watch on the arches until midnight, every other night. The other nights, I lie awake listening anyway.
My job's simple: no drowned past the arches. Everything else is gossip and polishing.
I train on the dummy every morning. It's never once complained, and it's won a few. Don't tell anyone.
Riding the reef is half the work. From a nautilus you spot a drowned early. From the ground you spot it late.
If the conch blows twice, I'm the first thing you'll see. Then the drowned, behind me, regretting things.
I check every lamp at dusk. A dark lamp is a gap, and a gap is where the drowned come through.
The singers brew me night-eyes for the watch. The dark goes grey and the drowned go bright. Tastes like old kelp, but it works.
I teach the fry to throw tridents. Little ones, blunt. They're terrifying. One of them got me in the tail last week. So proud.
A warden keeps their trident sharp, their armour tight and their nautilus fed. In that order, unless the nautilus is hungry. Then the nautilus.
When the drowned come in numbers, the conch sounds and every warden swims for the arches. We've never lost one yet. The arch, I mean. Well, either.
I patrol the gardens too. Seadragons can't fight. They just pretend to be kelp and hope. Somebody has to hope for them.
Training's not about being strong. It's about being where you're needed before you're needed there.
My armour is shell over leather over hope. The shellwright says the hope's the weakest layer. I say it's the most important.
Want to help? Keep your eyes open on the shelf road, and tell me if anything grey is walking where it shouldn't.
young.adventure: Will you tell me what is out past the lamps? I am not allowed. You are. That is not fair, but tell me anyway.
If you go to the old halls, will you look at them for me? Only look. And then tell me what colour the light is.
The Eyeguards say the Unseeing have two eyes like you but see nothing. I think that is sad. I would rather have one and see everything.
When you go out in the deep, keep a lamp with you. That is a rule. I made it up, but it is a good one.
If you meet a guardian, do not stare at it. That is what everybody tells me. I think it is because guardians are better at staring than us, and it is embarrassing.
Bring me back something from the land. Anything! I have never held anything that has been in the sun, except a breath-stone, and that does not count.
young.chat: Can you look at two things at once? Really at once? I tried, with one eye, and it just went sideways.

I am practising the stillness. You sit by the jelly pond and you do not move and you do not blink, and if you are still enough a glowjelly drifts against you. None has yet. I think they can tell when I am thinking about it.
My spines are still soft. When I come of count they will set hard, like the grown ones'. Then I will look very fierce. I practise fierce in the pond.
I have a toy guardian. It is made of prismarine and it has a little eye. It does not bite. Real ones bite. I am not allowed to go and see one.
Do your kind have counts? When I first felt the pull in my spines, I was given my number. I will not tell you it. You have to be a very good friend first.
What is the sun like? Is it a big glowjelly? Does it sting?
The grown ones will not tell us about the Silence. I asked an Archivist, and their spines went up so fast that I said sorry before they answered.
How do you breathe air? Where does it go? Does it just sit inside you?
I want to be an Eyeguard. Or a Lightwright. Or an Archivist. Or the one who looks after the jellies. I have decided to be all of them, one after another, slowly.
The merfolk fry came down to the court once, and they were so fast! They swam round the spire twice before I finished saying hello.
Is it true that on land things fall down instead of floating? Everything? Even you? Even lamps?
I counted all the lamps in {place}. Then I counted them again and got a different number. The Archivists say this is why we write things down.
When I am old I will know the whole Long Tide by heart. I already know the beginning: "I see you, Two-Eyes. Hear the Long Tide as the Oldest have always told it." That part is easy.
I watched a glowjelly split in two once. The whole thing! Nobody believed me. Then an Archivist wrote it down, so now it is true.
Why do you blink so much? Are your eyes very dry? Do they get tired of looking?
I am going to see the old halls one day. Not inside. Just from far away. The Eyeguards say maybe, when I am older. They say it very slowly, which means no.
Is it true you only have one name? We do too! But we have a court as well. You can borrow ours. "{player} of {place}." See? It fits.
I tried to stay awake as long as an Eyeguard. I fell asleep sitting up. Everyone said that counted as the stillness. I do not think it did.
young.chat.close: {player}, when I come of count and my spines set, will you come and see? I want you there. You can blink as much as you like.
I told the glowjellies about you. They did not say anything. They never do. But they drifted closer, so I think they approve.
You are my favourite Two-Eyes, {player}. You are also the only one I know. But you would be my favourite anyway.
I gave my toy guardian your name. It does not suit it. It is fierce and you are kind. I kept the name anyway.
I will tell you my count, {player}. Not yet. But I have decided. Deciding is the big part.
young.chat.new: You are the first Two-Eyes I have ever seen up close. You have so many eyes. Two is a lot.
Can I look at you for a while? I will be very still. You will not even notice. You are noticing. Sorry.
My name is {name}. When you have visited a lot, I will be allowed to call you by yours. I hope you visit a lot.
young.greet: I see you! I mean: I see you. Calmly. I am practising.
I see you! Is it true your kind close both eyes to sleep? Both at once?
I see you. My spines went up a little. They are still soft, so it does not count.
I see you! Wait. Let me be still first. There. I see you.
I see you. Did you come from the sun? What is it like? Is it loud?
I see you! I have been watching the glowjellies all tide and you are much more interesting. Do not tell them.
I see you. {elder} says I must not stare. I am not staring. I am seeing. It is different.
I see you! You can say "and I you". That is the polite answer. I only learned it last turning.
I see you. I am being very grown-up today. Can you tell? You can tell.
young.greet.friend: {player}! I see you! I have been counting your visits in my own count. It is up to a lot.
I see you, {player}! I held the stillness for half a tide yesterday. Nearly. Almost half.
{player}, I see you! Will you watch the glowjellies with me? You do not have to be still. I will be still for both of us.
I see you, {player}. I blinked slowly at you. That means I like you. You are supposed to know that now.
young.greet.stranger: A Two-Eyes! A real one! I see you! Sorry. I see you.
I see you, Two-Eyes. Which eye do you use for looking? Both? How do you choose?
I see you, Two-Eyes. I am not supposed to talk to strangers, but you are a guest, and guests are different. I think.
I see you, Two-Eyes. Are you lost? You do not look lost. You look lost but brave about it.
young.heart: Sometimes I worry I will never hold the stillness long enough. Then I worry that worrying is moving. Then I give up and watch the jellies.
I want to make the grown ones proud. Mostly I make them sigh. A sigh is a kind of proud, I think. A slow kind.
When my spines go up I feel ashamed, because everyone can see. Do your kind have anything that shows how you feel? You go red, someone said. Is that worse?
I am glad you came. Not many people come here. I do not mind the quiet. I just like it better with you in it.
I do not want to stop counting, ever. I told the Oldest Eye. The Oldest blinked slowly at me and said: good, then.
young.held.bucket: Is there a jelly in there? Can I see? I will be still. I am very good at being still near jellies. Nearly very good.
young.held.pearl: A Tidepearl! From the merfolk? It is so round. Everything they make is round. Everything we make is pointy.
young.held.prismarine: Prismarine! Watch: it changes colour if you look long enough. Do not blink. You blinked.
I am going to make a lamp from that one day. A tiny one. For a jelly to sleep under.
young.held.seal: Is that the Seal? The real one? An Oldest Eye gave you that? Can I touch it? I will not. I just wanted to ask.
The old beasts will know it! That is what the Long Tide says. Will you tell me if they do? Will you tell me what they look like up close?
young.held.trident: A trident! Can I hold it? No? Can I look at it very hard? Thank you.
When I am an Eyeguard, my trident will be called Stillness. Because it will be very fast. That is a joke. Kind of.
young.joke: What do you call a glowjelly that will not glow? A jelly. That is my best joke. I made it.
Why did the sponge go to the Archive? To soak up knowledge. The Archivist did not laugh. Their spines did, a little.
I tried to wink like you do. I just closed my eye. Then I could not see anything and I swam into a lamp.
How many eyes does a Two-Eyes have? Two! That is why they are called that! I worked it out myself.
Knock knock. Oh. We do not have doors. That is the end of the joke. I think it is funnier that way.
If the Eyeguards watch the court, who watches the Eyeguards? Me! I watch them all day. They hate it.
What is a guardian's favourite game? Staring. They always win. That is not a joke, really. It is true.
young.night: I am not supposed to be up. I am practising the stillness. In bed. It is very hard to tell from sleeping.
I like the evenings best, because the Long Tide gets told. The night is just the part after, when I am supposed to remember it.
The Eyeguards watch all night. I asked if they get scared. They said no. Their spines said a little bit.
When I cannot sleep I count the lamps through the window. I always fall asleep before I finish. One day I will finish.
young.past: In the Long Tide we lived in the great halls, and they were full of light and song. That is the beginning of the Long Tide. I know it by heart. The middle part I am still learning.
The halls had names like the Hall of Spines and the Deep Gate. I like the Hall of Spines best. It sounds like my crest when I am cross.
We used to have guardians as watch-beasts. Real ones. I asked if we could have one again, and everyone went very quiet.
I asked what the Silence was. Everyone said "later". It has been later for a very long time.
There was an Oldest called Ossiveth, who led everybody out of the halls and only looked back once. I asked what Ossiveth saw. That is another "later".
young.work: Watching the glowjellies. It is very important. If nobody watches them, they might do something and nobody would know.
I am watching the jellies for the Spongekeeper. They drift left, then right, then left. I am remembering it all down.
Practising the stillness. You are not supposed to talk while you practise. So I am not practising right now. I am explaining.
I am helping! I carried a lamp to the Pact crate. It was heavy. I did not drop it. Nearly, but not.
I am learning the Reckoning of Tides. One tide, a rising and a falling. Two tides, a day. Twenty-eight, a turning. Thirteen turnings... wait. A Long Count! I knew it.
I am feeling for the pull. You can feel it in your spines if you are very still. Can you feel it? In your... what do you have? Elbows?
The jelly by the far wall has not moved for a whole tide. It is either asleep or better at the stillness than me. Probably both.
I am counting sea pickles. Some have four lights and some have one. I like the ones with one. They are trying hard.
